peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response: We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. In response, we have included
additional mechanistic data to support the proposed model of action of 225 and in vivo evidence
demonstrating its potential for clinical development, which has significantly strengthened our
work.
Point-to-point response to reviewers
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
General Assessment:
Yan et al. describe the identification of NCATS-225 as an ERAD inhibitor via a GFP-
based HTS and elucidate its mechanism involving VDAC binding, dysregulation of
calcium homeostasis, and selective cancer cell cytotoxicity. While the study identifies a
novel compound with an intriguing mechanism and therapeutic potential, several critical
conclusions lack sufficient experimental validation. The mechanistic claims require
substantial reinforcement to meet the journal's standards. Major revisions addressing
the following points are essential prior to reconsideration.
Major Concerns:
1. HTS Compound Prioritization Rationale: The manuscript states that 6 compounds
were prioritized from 62 initial hits for further study. The specific criteria (e.g., potency,
chemical tractability, structural diversity, lack of known liabilities) guiding this selection
must be explicitly defined. Without this justification, the rationale for focusing on 225
remains unclear and potentially arbitrary.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We have revised the text to clarify
the selection rationale. The six compounds were prioritized from 62 confirmed hits based on
potency (AC50 < 20 μM), structural diversity, absence of covalent warheads or acute
cytotoxicity, and chemical tractability for optimization. The revised text (Results section, page
4) and updated Figs. 1d, e and S1d,e now explicitly describe this prioritization process.
2. Mechanism of STIM1-PERK Affinity Enhancement (Fig 8e): The observation that
225 enhances endogenous STIM1-PERK affinity is significant. However, as 225 is not
proposed to directly bind either protein, the underlying mechanism for this effect
remains entirely speculative. The authors must propose and experimentally test a
plausible mechanism (e.g., involving Ca2 flux, ER stress sensor activation, or
+
intermediary adaptors) or significantly temper their interpretation of this result.
Response: We agree the Reviewer that the mechanism must be explicit. Our new data support
a Ca2+-driven model in which 225 acts at VDAC1 to remodel ER–mitochondria signaling and
thereby increases STIM1–PERK affinity.
1) Direct target and Ca2+ remodeling: Photoaffinity labeling/mass spectrometry and new
results from CETSA and MST identify VDAC1 as the direct target (Figs. 4–5). In in vitro
reconstituted assay using recombinant VDAC1, 225 shifts VDAC1 to a lower-conductance
(“closed”) state that favors mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5c-e). This perturbs ER Ca2+ and
elicits compensatory Ca2+ influx, resulting in elevation of both ER and cytosolic Ca2+.
2) Complex remodeling requires Ca2+: Our data showed that under basal conditions, VDAC1 co-
immunoprecipitates with STIM1, PERK, and IP3R (Fig. 10j). Upon 225 treatment, VDAC1– IP3R
interaction increased, whereas VDAC1–STIM1 and VDAC1–PERK associations decreased (Fig.
10j), coinciding with enhanced PERK–STIM1 interaction (Figs. 10e, 10k). Notably, the 225-
induced increases in VDAC1–IP3R and PERK–STIM1 interactions were abolished by Ca2+
chelation (Figs. 9h, 10k). Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of PERK did not prevent the
225-induced PERK–STIM1 interaction (Fig. 10l), indicating that elevated intracellular Ca2+,
rather than PERK catalytic activity, drives the enhanced PERK–STIM1 association.
Working model: Under resting conditions, a PERK–STIM1 complex associates with VDAC1 and
limits VDAC1–IP3R coupling. By altering VDAC1 gating, 225 promotes Ca2+ flux that
strengthens PERK–STIM1 association and releases them from VDAC1, enabling enhanced
VDAC1–IP3R interaction. This explains the observed co-IP changes and the rise in PERK–
STIM1 interaction (Fig. 10e, j, k). We have revised the text and model (Fig. 11) to reflect this
mechanism and anchored our interpretation to the new Ca2+-dependence and co-IP data.
3. Clarity on ERAD Reporter Substrate (Fig 1e): The misfolded CD3δ-based drGFP
reporter used for secondary HTS validation must be clearly defined upon its first
mention in the main text (HTS section). Ensure consistent nomenclature between
text and Fig 1e.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for highlighting this point. We have now clearly defined
the misfolded CD3δ-based drGFP reporter upon its first mention in the HTS section (page 4)
and ensured consistent nomenclature between the main text and Figure 1e.
4. Validation of VDAC1-3 Binding: The identification of VDAC1-3 as targets via
photoaffinity labeling (PAL) and SDS-PAGE/MS is a key finding. However, confirmation
using orthogonal, quantitative biophysical methods is crucial to establish binding affinity,
specificity, and stoichiometry. Strongly recommend performing Cellular Thermal Shift
Assay (CETSA) combined with either Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) or Surface
Plasmon Resonance (SPR) to validate and quantify the direct interaction between 225
and VDAC isoforms 1-3. Relying solely on PAL (inherently detecting covalent
interactions) is insufficient proof of the physiological, non-covalent binding implied in the
proposed mechanism.
Response: We have validated 225 binding to all three VDAC isoforms using orthogonal biophysical
and functional approaches. CETSA analysis confirmed engagement of VDAC1–3 in cells (Fig. 5b).
In an in vitro reconstitution system, 225 modulated the gating activity of recombinant VDAC1 (Figs.
5c–e), providing functional evidence of direct interaction. Microscale thermophoresis (MST)
further demonstrated a direct, high-affinity interaction between 225 and purified VDAC1 (Fig. 5a).
Although recombinant VDAC2 and VDAC3 proteins were not available for MST analysis, the
consistent CETSA results across all isoforms, combined with functional and quantitative binding
data for VDAC1, provide strong evidence that 225 directly engages all three VDAC isoforms.
5. Incomplete Exploration of Differential Cell Sensitivity: The differential sensitivity of
cancer cell lines to 225 is a compelling observation with translational relevance. However,
the exploration of the proposed mechanism (involving ERAD/ER-phagy crosstalk) is
superficial. To validate the hypothesis that ER-phagy capacity dictates sensitivity, the
authors should inhibit ER-phagy (e.g., via genetic knockdown of key regulators like
FAM134B, SEC62, or CCPG1, or using pharmacological inhibitors like CQ/HCQ where
appropriate) in resistant/low-sensitivity cell lines and assess whether this sensitizes them
to 225-induced cytotoxicity. Demonstrating this functional link is essential to support the
model in Figure 9.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the mechanistic basis of
differential cellular sensitivity to 225. We agree that this is an important question with clear
translational relevance. In our original submission, we demonstrated that sensitivity to 225
correlates with a prolonged and dysregulated increase in intracellular calcium. Given that
VDAC1 is the primary target of 225 and is highly expressed in cancers, we investigated whether
VDAC1 expression levels contribute to the observed differences in sensitivity. Notably, our new
data showed that VDAC1 protein levels were generally higher in 225-sensitive cells and lower in
insensitive or normal cells (Fig. 8d, e). However, one insensitive line (MDA-MB-231) displayed
unexpectedly high VDAC1 expression (Fig. 8d, e), suggesting additional regulatory mechanisms
may be involved. We speculate that mutations affecting downstream death-signaling pathways
may account for this discrepancy. Collectively, these data suggest that VDAC1 abundance
influences the extent of 225-induced calcium dysregulation, contributing to differential cellular
sensitivity.
We would like to clarify that our working model does not posit that “ER-phagy capacity dictates
sensitivity.” Rather, our data indicate that VDAC1 normally restrains ER-phagy activation, since
VDAC1 knockdown leads to ER-phagy induction (Fig. 4f-g). This increase in ER-phagy, in turn,
accelerates the clearance of ERAD substrates (Fig. 4h, i), which may reduce substrate
availability for dislocation and thereby dampen downstream stress signaling.
Based on our current data, ER-phagy capacity does not appear to drive the differential sensitivity
to 225. Therefore, experiments such as genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of ER-phagy in
resistant cell lines would not directly test our model at this stage. Instead, our findings
consistently implicate 225-induced disruption of calcium homeostasis as the key differentiating
factor and its target (VDAC1) expression levels are likely to contribute to the sensitivity
differences among cancer cell lines. Thus, the lower levels of VDAC1 expression in normal cells
may explain why 225 is not toxic to normal cells. Overall, calcium dysregulation, not ER-phagy
capacity, remains the most plausible driver of sensitivity. Our new data on VDAC1 protein
interactions and 225s’ impact substantially advance our understanding of its mechanism of
action and will guide future studies of differential toxicity. Because calcium regulation is highly
complex, we believe that fully defining the mechanism lies beyond the scope of this study.
6. Lack of In Vivo Efficacy and Safety Data: Demonstrating potent and selective cancer
cell killing in vitro is promising, but in vivo validation is a fundamental requirement for a
mechanistic/therapeutic study of this nature in Nature Communications. The authors
should provide evidence of 225's efficacy in relevant tumor xenograft or syngeneic
models, alongside assessment of toxicity in normal tissues. This is critical for
establishing the compound's therapeutic window and translational potential.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of in vivo validation to
establish the translational potential of 225. We have now added new in vivo data into the revised
manuscript (Fig. 7c-e and S7g-i). Specifically, 225 significantly inhibits tumor growth in the
A375 xenograft mouse model (Fig. 7c-e). Importantly, treated animals showed no clinical signs
of toxicity, and histopathological analysis of liver, pancreas, and kidney revealed no abnormality
(Fig. S7g-i). These results demonstrate both the anti-tumor efficacy and favorable safety profile
of 225 in vivo, thereby supporting its translational relevance.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study by Yan et al., the authors developed a chemical screening platform based
on an ERAD dislocation reporter. The screen identified compound 225 as a small-
molecule ERAD inhibitor. They further dissected the mechanism of action of 225 by
identifying the VDACs as the drug targets, demonstrating disruption of calcium
homeostasis, and linking the PERK/STIM1 axis to degradation of ERAD complex
proteins and cell death. Overall, this is an interesting study that provides novel insights
into the regulation of UPR, calcium homeostasis, ERAD, and ER-phagy.
Several minor comments are listed below:
1. Figure 3a: The authors mentioned the degradation of OS9, HERP1, and FAM8A1.
However, the data also show a reduction in SEL1L at 24 hours post-treatment. This
should also be noted in the text.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have updated the manuscript
to include the observed reduction in SEL1L at 24 hours post-treatment (page 5)..
2. Figure 3: The authors should examine transcriptomic changes in the RNA-seq data
for OS9, HERP1, FAM8A1, and SEL1L mRNA levels to rule out mRNA downregulation
as the cause of decreased protein levels.
Response: We have added the RNA-seq data as requested by the Reviewer (Fig. S3b). 225 slightly
increased HERP1 and OS9 mRNA, slightly decreased FAM8A1 mRNA, and caused no changes in
SEL1L mRNA. These data ruled out mRNA downregulation as the cause of decreased protein
levels. In addition, we have shown that HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 downregulation is due to
proteasomal degradation likely via ERAD in our first submission (Fig. S3a, c).
3. Figures 2d–g and 4i: Treatment with 225 significantly inhibited the degradation of
both NHK and CD3, resulting in increased protein levels. However, in Figure 4i,
siVDAC1 treatment reduced CD3-mCherry levels. These findings seem
inconsistent and should be clarified.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We would like to clarify that the effects
of siVDAC1 on CD3δ-mCherry shown in Figure 4i are mechanistically distinct from those of
225. Specifically, VDAC1 knockdown induces ER-phagy, which accelerates the clearance of
ERAD substrates such as CD3δ-mCherry. In contrast, treatment with 225 inhibits ERAD,
leading to stabilization and accumulation of CD3δ-mCherry. Thus, the apparent discrepancy
reflects two different mechanisms of action rather than inconsistent data.
4. The term “dislocation” should be defined earlier in the manuscript for clarity.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have now defined “dislocation” in
the first paragraph of the Introduction as part of our ERAD description: “ER-associated
degradation (ERAD) is a key quality-control pathway in which misfolded proteins in the
endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are recognized, retrotranslocated to the cytosolic surface for
ubiquitination and dislocation, and subsequently delivered to the proteasome for
degradation.”(page 2). This introduces the term at first mention and aligns with its usage
throughout the manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Yan and colleagues present compelling evidence that stress-induced apoptosis in
cancer cells can be increased by suppressing the Endoplasmic Reticulum-Associated
Degradation (ERAD) pathway using small molecules. Through an extensive drug
screening campaign employing a clever designed readout, they identified novel ERAD
inhibitors. One of the most potent molecules identified, compound 225, not only inhibits
ERAD but also binds the mitochondrial porin VDAC1. While a direct link between VDAC1
and the ERAD pathway has not been conclusively established before, the authors
provide strong evidence supporting VDAC1 involvement in ERAD regulation.
The manuscript is data-rich and covers several key aspects, including the drug
screening process, interaction studies (IP experiments), and mechanistic insights
that collectively support the proposed conclusions. However, I have several
important questions and concerns that should be addressed prior to publication:
Major Points:
1. The authors demonstrate that compound 225 stabilizes the interaction between
VDAC1 and the IP3 receptor. Do the authors have mechanistic insights or supporting
data explaining why this interaction is enhanced in the presence of molecule 225? Is
this effect direct, or could it result from broader changes in organelle physiology?
Response: We agree that a mechanistic explanation is needed. Our new data support a VDAC1-
centric, Ca2+-dependent mechanism by which 225 enhances the VDAC1–IP3R interaction.
1) Direct target and Ca2+ remodeling: Photoaffinity labeling/mass spectrometry and new results
from CETSA and MST identify VDAC1 as the direct target (Figs. 4–5). In in vitro reconstituted
assay using recombinant VDAC1, 225 shifts VDAC1 to a lower-conductance (“closed”) state
that favors mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5c-e). This perturbs ER Ca2+ and elicits
compensatory Ca2+ influx, resulting in elevation of both ER and cytosolic Ca2+.
2) Complex remodeling requires Ca2+: Our data showed that under basal conditions, VDAC1 co-
immunoprecipitates with STIM1, PERK, and IP3R (Fig. 10j). Upon 225 treatment, VDAC1– IP3R
interaction increased, whereas VDAC1–STIM1 and VDAC1–PERK associations decreased (Fig.
10j), coinciding with enhanced PERK–STIM1 interaction (Figs. 10e, 10k). Notably, the 225-
induced increases in VDAC1–IP3R and PERK–STIM1 interactions were abolished by Ca2+
chelation (Figs. 9h, 10k). Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of PERK did not prevent the
225-induced PERK–STIM1 interaction (Fig. 10l), indicating that elevated intracellular Ca2+,
rather than PERK catalytic activity, drives the enhanced PERK–STIM1 association.

limits VDAC1–IP3R coupling. By altering VDAC1 gating, 225 promotes Ca2+ flux that
strengthens PERK–STIM1 association and releases them from VDAC1, enabling enhanced
VDAC1–IP3R interaction. This explains the observed co-IP changes and the rise in PERK–
STIM1 interaction (Fig. 10e, j, k). We have revised the text and model (Fig. 11) to reflect this
mechanism and anchored our interpretation to the new Ca2+-dependence and co-IP data.
Functional model: This alteration in VDAC] protein interactions yields two modules: VDAC]–
IP3R (facilitating mitochondrial Ca2+ transfer) and PERK–STIM] (ERAD inhibition), aligning
with our phenotypic readouts.
2. Compound 225 appears to have dual effects: it activates PERK, resulting in STIM1
phosphorylation, HERP1 degradation, and ERAD inhibition; while also binding to
VDAC1. However, UV-crosslinking identified VDACs as the only direct targets. How
do the authors reconcile this dual activity? Is there evidence that the STIM1–PERK
interaction is influenced by the VDAC–IP3R complex? Could the authors attempt IP
experiments to pull down VDAC using STIM1 or PERK in the presence of 225 to test
for complex formation?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s question. We reconcile the apparent “dual activity”
with a single-target model: 225 directly engages VDACs, and the PERK/STIM] phenotypes arise
secondarily from VDAC-driven Ca2+ remodeling at ER–mitochondria contact sites and
subsequently disruption of calcium homeostasis. Consistent with this, photoaffinity labeling
identifies VDAC]–3 as the only direct targets (Fig. 4a-c); CETSA shows thermal stabilization of
VDACs (Fig. 5b); MST confirms binding to recombinant VDAC] (Fig. 5a); and an in vitro
reconstituted VDAC] channel assay demonstrates 225-dependent gating modulation (Fig. 5c-e).
In addition, we do not detect 225 binding to PERK or STIM] by photoaffinity labeling (Fig. 4a-
c).
To determine whether the STIM]–PERK interaction is influenced by the VDAC–IP3R complex,
we performed co-immunoprecipitations using VDAC] as bait. VDAC] co-precipitated IP3R,
STIM], and PERK (Fig. ]0j). Treatment with 225 increased VDAC]–IP3R association while
decreasing VDAC] interactions with STIM] and PERK (Fig. ]0j). Interestingly, in first
submission, we showed that 225 enhanced the STIM]–PERK interaction (Fig. ]0e). Now we
show that both the 225-induced VDAC]–IP3R association and STIM]–PERK interaction was
attenuated by intracellular Ca2+ chelation (BAPTA-AM) (Fig. 9h, ]0k), indicating Ca2+
dependence. Collectively, these data led us to propose the working model described earlier:
under resting conditions, a PERK–STIM] complex associates with VDAC] and limits VDAC]–
IP3R coupling. By altering VDAC] gating, 225 promotes Ca2+ flux that strengthens PERK–
STIM] association and releases them from VDAC], enabling enhanced VDAC]–IP3R
interaction. Functionally, blocking IP3R or knocking down MCU reduces 225-associated
cytotoxicity, consistent with a role for the VDAC–IP3R–MCU axis in propagating mitochondrial
Ca2+ uptake and downstream effects.
3. The manuscript claims that molecule 225 selectively targets cancer cells without
affecting healthy cells. Given that VDAC1 is overexpressed in many solid tumors, did
the authors assess VDAC1 expression levels in 225-sensitive versus -insensitive cell
lines? Quantifying VDAC1 levels by RNA-seq and Western blot would help clarify
whether sensitivity to 225 correlates with VDAC1 expression and might explain the
lack of toxicity in healthy cells.
Response: We agree this is an important question with clear translational relevance. As
suggested by the reviewer, we examined VDAC1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels
in 225-sensitive versus -insensitive cell lines. We found that VDAC1 protein levels are generally
higher in sensitive cells and lower in insensitive and normal cells (Fig. 8d,e), although one
insensitive line (MDA-MB-231) exhibited unexpectedly high VDAC1 protein levels. We observed
no correlation between VDAC1 transcript abundance (analyzed public RNA-seq datasets
(https://www.proteinatlas.org) and protein levels (Fig. 8d,e vs. Fig. S8a), indicating that steady-
state VDAC1 protein abundance is likely regulated by translational efficiency or protein
stability rather than mRNA expression. Consistent with this, treatment of HeLa cells (a sensitive
line) with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib stabilized VDAC1 protein (Fig. S8b), suggesting
that VDAC1 is an unstable protein subject to proteasomal degradation. Taken together, these
findings indicate that VDAC1 protein abundance, rather than mRNA expression alone,
contributes to the differential sensitivity to 225.
4. The authors propose that molecule 225 enhances VDAC1–IP3R interaction,
promoting calcium transfer between the ER and mitochondria, which subsequently
activates PERK and drives ERAD inhibition. However, this does not fully explain the
observed increase in cytosolic calcium (Fig. 7c). Could the authors comment on the
source of the cytosolic calcium and clarify whether this increase is a direct or indirect
consequence of 225 treatment?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s question. We added new experiment using in vitro
reconstituted VDAC1 gating assay and found that 225 shifts VDAC1 into a “closed” state
favoring mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5), which is consistent with our observations that
225 increases VDAC1-IP3R interaction and calcium influx to mitochondria. We propose that
the mitochondrial calcium influx transiently lowers ER Ca2+, triggering compensatory Ca2+
influx from the extracellular space into the cytosol. The resulting elevation of cytosolic calcium
replenishes ER stores and ultimately increases calcium across the ER, cytosol, and
mitochondria, resulting in compartment-wide Ca2+ elevation, as shown in our first
submission. This model of action for 225 are supported by new data
5. The small molecule efsevin has been shown to stabilize the calcium-conductive
form of VDAC1 (PMID: 32059260). It would be informative to compare the effects of
efsevin and compound 225 on ERAD inhibition. Do both compounds share a similar
mechanism of action? Such a comparison might strengthen the proposed model.
Response: As suggested by the reviewer, we compared efsevin with compound 225 for their
effects on dislocation inhibition and on degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1. Efsevin
showed no detectable effect on dislocation or on degradation of these ERAD complex proteins
(Fig. S2a,b), indicating that its mechanism of action differs from that of compound 225.
Minor Points:
Scheme on Figure 8j should be revised to clearly depict relevant subcellular
compartments, improve image quality, and remove the pink background. Additionally,
the graph located at the bottom left appears to be an error and should be removed.
Response: The scheme has been revised as requested to clearly depict the relevant subcellular
compartments, improve image quality, and remove the pink background. The erroneous graph
at the bottom left has also been removed. The updated version now appears as Figure 11.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Key Results
This manuscript identifies a novel small molecule, NCATS-225 (“225”), as a selective
ERAD inhibitor that binds to voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs). Through a
combination of high-content screening, biochemical validation, and mechanistic
dissection, the authors suggest that 225 triggers an intracellular calcium imbalance via
a VDAC-IP3R-PERK-STIM1 signaling axis. This leads to the degradation of ERAD
complex components (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1) and induces cell death selectively in
cancer cells while sparing normal cells. The work uncovers a previously unrecognized
role for VDACs in ERAD regulation and presents a compelling chemical probe for
further study of ER proteostasis and cancer-selective cytotoxicity.
Validity
The data are of high quality, robust, and generally well-controlled. The experimental
workflow is thorough, including orthogonal validation of dislocation inhibition (GFP
reporters, CHX chase, ubiquitination assays), target identification (photoaffinity labeling
and MS), and functional studies using gene knockouts and chemical inhibitors.
However, the precise mechanism of 225 binding to VDACs and how this affects VDAC
function at a structural level remains speculative. The authors acknowledge this and
propose it as future work.
Response: Thank you for the positive assessment. In this revision, we add new evidence of direct
225–VDAC engagement by CETSA and MST (Fig. 5), complementing the photoaffinity
labeling/MS from the initial submission (Fig. 4). We also show in a reconstituted VDAC1 assay
that 225 shifts channel gating toward a lower-conductance (“closed”) state that favors
mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5). We acknowledge that the atomic binding mode and
structural basis of this effect remain to be defined and outline these as future work.
Significance
The identification of a VDAC-targeting small molecule that selectively disrupts ERAD
and kills cancer cells is novel and potentially impactful. This work opens new avenues
in cancer biology, proteostasis, and chemical biology. It also proposes an alternative
strategy to targeting UPR sensors directly — by modulating ERAD upstream. The
selective toxicity of 225 to certain cancer cell lines suggests translational relevance.
While the mechanistic basis of this selectivity is not fully resolved, the dataset
lays a solid foundation for follow-up studies.
Response: Thank you for the thoughtful comments. We agree the work is novel and impactful. In
this revision, we began to address the basis of selectivity by quantifying VDAC1 at both mRNA
and protein levels in 225-sensitive versus -insensitive lines. Protein abundance was generally
higher in sensitive lines and lower in insensitive or normal cells (Fig. 8d,e), with one outlier
(MDA-MB-231) showing high VDAC1 despite relative insensitivity. By contrast, VDAC1
transcripts from public RNA-seq (Human Protein Atlas) did not correlate with protein levels or
sensitivity (Fig. S8a). In HeLa cells, the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib stabilized VDAC1
protein (Fig. S8b), consistent with proteasomal turnover. Together, these data suggest that
VDAC1 protein abundance contributes to 225 selectivity, but additional factors must be
involved and warrants future investigations.
Data and Methodology
The methodology is state-of-the-art and spans a wide range of experimental techniques,
including high-content screening, SAR chemistry, CRISPR knockouts, calcium imaging,
and GSEA transcriptomic profiling. The description of materials and methods is detailed
and transparent. Use of the drGFP reporter for dislocation, combined with dose-
responses, time courses, and structure–activity relationships, makes the data solid.
Photoaffinity labeling with mass spectrometry is well executed, and VDAC target
identification is convincing. If available, raw calcium traces or proteomics data could be
made public in supplementary datasets.
Response: All source data for figures have been submitted in this resubmission. No
additional datasets need to be made available in public database.
Analytical Approach
Quantitative results are consistently supported by replicates, appropriate statistical
tests, and careful normalization. The use of dose-response curves, IC50 values, and
multiple replicates is appropriate. GSEA is correctly applied and complements the
mechanistic data. The authors have been transparent about sample sizes and
statistical significance thresholds.
Suggested Improvements
The authors present a compelling study identifying VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as
direct binding partners of compound 225. They propose that 225 perturbs calcium
homeostasis at the ER-mitochondria interface via these outer mitochondrial membrane
proteins, thereby inhibiting ER-associated degradation (ERAD), activating the unfolded
protein response (UPR), and triggering apoptosis. While the data are generally sound
and well-presented, I believe an alternative, structurally grounded interpretation offers a
more parsimonious explanation of the experimental findings.
Recent structural studies (Li et al., Aging 2023, DOI:10.18632/aging.205660) demonstrate that VDAC1 directly binds the ER
membrane protein complex (EMC) at ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs), locking the EMC in a non-insertase
conformation.
Earlier proteomic mapping
(Christianson, J., Olzmann, J., Shaler, T. et al. Defining human ERAD networks through an integrative mapping strategy. Nat
Cell Biol 14, 93–105 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1038/ncb2383)
showed that multiple EMC subunits interact with Derlin-1 and Derlin-2, core components of the ERAD dislocation
machinery. This raises the possibility that compound 225 inhibits ERAD not by modulating VDAC channel activity directly,
but by stabilizing a non-functional EMC–VDAC complex that disrupts EMC-dependent membrane insertion of ERAD
components such as Derlin-1.
Below, I analyze the major data types presented by the authors in support of their model and offer the alternative EMC-mediated interpretation.
1. Identification of VDAC1/2/3 as targets of 225:
The authors used a clickable photoaffinity analog of 225 to identify VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as binding targets. This result is compatible with both their interpretation (VDAC as a functional target for calcium flux regulation) and my alternative model (VDACs as structural partners of EMC, mediating 225 activity via this complex).
2. Inhibition of ERAD and activation of UPR by 225:
225 blocks degradation of NHK and HA-DeltaF508CFTR, canonical ERAD substrates. It also induces expression of BiP, CHOP, and ATF4. The authors ascribe this to ER calcium dysregulation. However, a simpler model is that 225-bound VDAC stabilizes EMC in a non-insertase state, blocking the membrane integration of Derlin-1 and other EMC-dependent ERAD components, thereby directly impairing ERAD and triggering proteostatic stress. This hypothesis explains all observed consequences (ERAD block, UPR, cell death) without invoking a poorly defined Ca2+ channeling role for VDACs.
3. Triple VDAC1 KD / VDAC2-/- / VDAC3-/- cells resist 225 phenotypes:
The authors interpret this as evidence that VDACs are the functional conduits for calcium flux perturbed by 225. However, in the alternative model, the absence of VDACs prevents 225 from stabilizing the EMC–VDAC complex. This restores EMC function and Derlin-1 insertion, preserving ERAD and preventing downstream UPR and Ca2+ dysregulation. Thus, the triple KO phenotype is compatible with both models.
Responses to comment #1-3: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments. To test possible
EMC involvement in 225’s action, we performed a series of experiments. However, our
data do not support an EMC-mediated mechanism: (1) ERAD complex degradation persists with
EMC knockdown, 225 still caused degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in EMC3, EMC4,
and EMC7 knockdown cells, similar to controls (Fig. S4e); (2) the mitochondrial Ca2+ rise
induced by 225 is unchanged by EMC3/EMC4/EMC7 knockdown (Fig. S4h); (3) the dislocation
reporter is unaffected by EMC knockdown, EMC3 or EMC7 knockdown did not alter 225’s
inhibition in the drGFP assay (Fig. S4f); and (4) VDAC–EMC interactions are unchanged by
225, VDAC1 co-IP with EMC3 or EMC4 did not increase (Fig. S4g). Together, these results do
not support EMC as the mediator of 225 activity and instead align with direct VDAC targeting
and Ca2+-dependent remodeling at ER–mitochondria contact sites.
4. ER calcium flux and 225-induced cell death:
Calcium flux is clearly altered by 225, but the authors do not provide direct
electrophysiological or structural evidence that 225 opens or blocks VDAC pores. Given
that VDAC is primarily known as a metabolite channel in the outer mitochondrial
membrane, and that Ca2+ flow between ER and mitochondria typically involves IP3R-
GRP75-VDAC tethers, it remains uncertain whether VDAC alone mediates Ca2+ leak. In
contrast, the EMC-centered model predicts that ER stress and UPR activation are
primary, and that calcium dysregulation is a downstream effect of ER proteostasis
failure.
Response: We agree that direct functional evidence is essential. As noted above, EMC is not
involved in 225’s action. We provide orthogonal target engagement (photoaffinity labeling/MS,
CETSA, MST) showing that 225 binds VDAC1 (Figs. 4-5), and we add new data using a
reconstituted VDAC1 gating assay, demonstrating that 225 shifts the channel toward a lower-
conductance (“closed”) state that favors mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5d-e). Consistent with
ER–mitochondria tethers, 225 enhances VDAC1–IP3R association, and this remodeling is lost
with Ca2+ chelation (Figs. 9g–h, 10k). Taken together, these data support a VDAC-centered,
Ca2+-dependent mechanism for the observed flux changes and cell death, while single-channel
electrophysiology and structural mapping of the binding site remain future work.
Conclusion:
In light of published structural and proteomic data, the model in which compound 225
exerts its effects by stabilizing a non-insertase EMC–VDAC complex provides a
mechanistically unified explanation of all observed phenotypes: ERAD inhibition, UPR
activation, and calcium flux. It avoids invoking a direct gating effect of 225 on VDACs,
for which no structural or biophysical support is currently provided. I suggest the
authors consider this alternative mechanism in the discussion and test whether EMC
activity or Derlin-1 insertion is altered upon 225 treatment.
Response: Please refer Response to # 1-3 above.
This model is not incompatible with the authors' data, but may better contextualize the
role of VDACs as structural, rather than purely channel, components at MAMs. It also
makes distinct predictions about EMC dependency that could be experimentally tested.
Suggested experiments:
Assess Derlin-1 levels and membrane insertion after 225 treatment
Response: As noted above, EMC does not appear to mediate 225’s effects. Derlin-1 protein
levels were also not affected by 225 treatment (Fig. 3a); therefore, we did not assess Derlin-1
membrane insertion.
Test EMC–VDAC complex stability or conformation changes in the presence of 225
Response: We tested whether 225 alters EMC–VDAC complex stability or conformation. VDAC1
co-immunoprecipitation with EMC3 or EMC4 was unchanged in the presence of 225, indicating
no detectable effect on EMC–VDAC complex stability (Fig. S4g).
Compare 225 sensitivity in cells with EMC subunit knockdown or mutation
Response: We tested EMC involvement directly. Knockdown of EMC3, EMC4, or EMC7 did not
change (i) 225-induced degradation of ERAD complex proteins (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1), (ii) the
mitochondrial Ca2+ rise, or (iii) dislocation inhibition in the drGFP assay, and 225 did not
increase VDAC1 co-IP with EMC3/4 (Fig. S4). Because these activity-linked readouts were
unchanged, EMC loss did not appear to modulate 225 sensitivity; therefore, we did not pursue
additional viability assays in EMC-mutant backgrounds.
Clarity and Context
The manuscript is clearly written and accessible. Figures are well designed and support
the main conclusions. The discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within
existing literature and discusses limitations transparently. The novelty of VDACs in
ERAD is well supported.
References
The referencing is thorough and appropriate. Key prior work on ERAD, UPR, VDAC
function, and chemical screening is cited. I did not note any major omissions.
Your Expertise
My expertise includes ER proteostasis and chemical biology. I am confident in
assessing the main findings and mechanistic claims. I did not independently evaluate
the full MS data or chemical synthesis protocols but found the presented validation
to be sufficient.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed
reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in
peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers
who co-review manuscripts.
Response: Thank you for co-reviewing our manuscript as part of Nature Communications ’
initiative to train and recognize Early Career Researchers. We appreciate the time and
thoughtful evaluation from both you and your co-reviewer.
Point-to-point response to the Reviewers
We are grateful for the opportunity to resubmit our revised manuscript and sincerely thank
Reviewers #1, #2, #4, and #5 for their positive recommendations for acceptance in Nature
Communications. We also appreciate the constructive comments from Reviewer #3 and have
revised the data accordingly. We believe that the thoughtful feedback from all reviewers has
substantially improved the quality of the manuscript.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
I would like to thank the authors for their comprehensive response to my previous
comments. The additional data and revisions have significantly improved the
manuscript, and I am impressed with the work. I am happy to recommend the
manuscript for acceptance. Congratulations to the team on a fine piece of research!
Response:
We sincerely thank Reviewer #1 for the positive evaluation and encouraging comments. We
greatly appreciate your support and are pleased that the revisions have strengthened the
manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have successfully addressed my comments. No additional questions.
Response:
We thank Reviewer #2 for acknowledging that our revisions have addressed all prior comments.
We appreciate your time and consideration in reviewing our manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have satisfactorily addressed all my previous concerns, many of which
were also raised by the other reviewers. In particular, the additional experiments now
provide stronger support for their proposed working model. The revised data establish a
clear mechanism of action for compound 225, which stabilizes the VDAC1–IP3R
interaction at the expense of STIM1 and PERK association.
I appreciate the authors’ efforts to confirm the direct binding of 225 to VDAC1 using
orthogonal approaches, including electrophysiological assays that demonstrate an
effect on VDAC1 gating consistent with stabilization of its closed state. However, I have
one remaining point of clarification. The reported dissociation constant (Kd) of ~3 μM for
225–VDAC1 interaction (as determined by MST) suggests a moderate affinity. Given
this, why were the bilayer experiments performed using only 400 nM compound? At
such a concentration—well below the K_D—binding would be expected to be minimal.
Indeed, the dose–response curve in Figure 5a suggests little to no effect at this
concentration, yet the electrophysiological recordings show a measurable change in
G/G_max. While binding and functional efficacy are not necessarily identical processes,
binding must occur for an effect to be observed. How do the authors reconcile this
apparent discrepancy between binding affinity and electrophysiological response at sub-
Kd concentrations (200–400 nM)?
Along similar lines, in Figure 5c, the representative traces appear to have been acquired
at different voltages across the conditions (±60 mV for control, ±40 mV for 200 nM 225,
and ±30 mV for 400 nM 225). Could the authors clarify the rationale behind using
different potentials for each condition? For better comparison, I suggest presenting
representative traces recorded at the same voltages for all experimental conditions, or
alternatively including a supplemental figure showing the full voltage range. As currently
presented, it is difficult to directly appreciate the effect of compound 225 across
conditions in Figure 5c.
Response:
Our orthogonal validation demonstrates that compound 225 exhibits a highly favorable, context-
dependent mechanism of target engagement. We confirmed direct target engagement with a 3
µM binding affinity using Microscale Thermophoresis (MST). However, when we assessed the
compound in a physiologically relevant functional assay, using VDAC1 reconstituted into its
native membrane environment, we observed a significantly enhanced functional potency of 400
nM. This 7.5-fold increase in potency is a key finding. It indicates that the compound's activity is
optimized in the correct biological context. The most plausible explanation is a membrane-
induced conformational change: VDAC1 likely adopts its specific, functional conformation only
within a true lipid bilayer. 225 appears to have a much higher affinity for this active, membrane-
embedded state. The MST assay, which measures an average affinity across all conformations in
detergent, reports a weaker value. This model is strongly supported by our cellular data, which
shows an IC50 of 1 µM in inhibiting dislocation in cells, a context where VDAC1 is naturally
anchored in the lipid membrane. Therefore, we have high confidence that the sub-micromolar
potencies (400 nM - 1 µM) are the biologically and therapeutically relevant metrics,
demonstrating that our compound is a potent and functionally active inhibitor of VDAC1.
Following the Reviewer's helpful suggestion, we modified Figure 5c and present the single-
channel current traces at the same applied voltages from -30 to 60 mV for each condition. The
lowest voltages at which VDAC1 gating was observed in control and in the presence of 225 are
indicated by arrows.The corresponding discussion has been added to the revised manuscript
(page 12 in red).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
I am happy with (and impressed by!) the new data gathered and presented and I
recommend the manuscript for publication.
Response:
We thank Reviewer #4 for the positive and encouraging comments. We greatly appreciate your
recognition of the new data and are pleased that our revisions meet your expectations.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports.
This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review
and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Response:
We thank Reviewer #5 for the co-review and appreciate Nature Communications’ initiative to
support and recognize Early Career Researchers in the peer review process.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I thank the authors for their thorough and thoughtful response to my previous
comments. The additional data and revisions have substantially strengthened the
manuscript, and I am pleased with the improvements made. However, I noticed that the
scale bars in Fig. 5c are now missing, whereas they were present in the previous
version of the manuscript. Aside from this minor issue, I am happy to recommend the
manuscript for acceptance.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and positive evaluation of our work, as well
as for the helpful comments that have strengthened the manuscript. We apologize for the
oversight regarding Fig. 5c, and the missing scale bar has now been added in the revised version.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) is a critical protein quality control mechanism that also regulates lipid metabolism and calcium homeostasis. Dysregulation of ERAD and unfolded protein response underlies diseases including cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic syndromes. Small molecule modulators of ERAD could enable mechanistic discovery and therapeutic intervention, but few have been identified. Using a high-content screening, we discovered several ERAD-modulating compounds, including NCATS-SM0225, an ERAD inhibitor that unexpectedly binds all three isoforms of VDAC, outer mitochondrial membrane proteins enriched at mitochondria-associated membranes. This led us to discover an essential role for VDACs in ERAD and ER-phagy. NCATS-SM0225 elevates cytosolic, ER, and mitochondrial calcium through calcium influx and IP3R–MCU activity. This calcium imbalance strengthens VDAC1–IP3R coupling and activates PERK, which phosphorylates STIM1 and drives degradation of key ERAD regulators. Loss of these components amplifies PERK signaling and selectively kills cancer cells while sparing normal cells. These findings uncover a cancer-specific role of VDACs in ERAD regulation and calcium signaling, highlighting a therapeutically actionable vulnerability.

---

## Introduction

The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a central organelle responsible for protein folding, lipids synthesis, and calcium homeostasis, essential for maintaining cellular proteostasis. ER-associated degradation (ERAD) is a critical quality control mechanism in which misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are recognized, retrotranslocated to the cytosolic surface for ubiquitination and dislocation, and subsequently delivered to the proteasome for degradation1–6. Beyond protein quality control, ERAD also regulates physiological processes such as lipid metabolism and calcium signaling by selectively degrading transcription factors, enzymes, and regulatory proteins often in a cell type-specific manner3,7,8. ERAD is closely coordinated with ER-phagy, a selective autophagy process that degrades ER fragments and misfolded proteins, compensating for ERAD deficiencies and protecting the ER from dysfunction3,9,10. Insufficient removal and subsequent accumulation of misfolded proteins lead to ER stress and activates the unfolded protein response (UPR)11,12. The UPR is mediated by three ER stress sensors—IRE1α, ATF6, and PERK—which work to restore proteostasis. However, severe or prolonged ER stress can shift the UPR toward pro-apoptotic signaling13–15. While the UPR is critical for maintaining the function of secretory cells like pancreatic β-cells and B lymphocytes, it is also implicated in diseases such as cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic syndromes14,16–19.

In neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, Huntington’s, Parkinson’s and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, toxic protein aggregates disrupt ERAD, causing chronic ER stress and neuronal cell death via pro-apoptotic UPR signaling20–28. In contrast, cancer cells often experience ER stress due to disrupted protein homeostasis; in this context, the UPR is reprogrammed to promote survival, tumorigenesis, metastasis, drug resistance, and immune evasion16,18,29,30. UPR activation has been documented in many human cancers, including breast, pancreatic, lung, prostate, brain, and hematologic malignancies16,30. Small-molecule inhibitors targeting specific UPR branches have been developed to explore therapeutic potential but overlapping functions and compensatory mechanisms may limit their efficacies31,32.

Modulating ERAD activity represents a promising strategy to influence ER stress and UPR signaling, as misfolded protein accumulation is the primary driver of ER stress. Enhancing or inhibiting ERAD can either promote clearance or exacerbate accumulation of misfolded proteins, respectively, thereby shaping cellular stress responses31,33,34. The development of potent and selective small molecule ERAD modulators as chemical biology tools is an important step towards dissecting ERAD mechanisms and roles in physiology and disease. ERAD modulators also offer therapeutic potential by enhancing ERAD to alleviate ER stress in neurodegenerative diseases and diabetes or suppressing ERAD to sensitize cancer cells to stress-induced apoptosis33–35. However, only a limited number of ERAD modulators have been identified to date, and the field remains underdeveloped.

In this study, we present the development of a high-content phenotypic screening assay designed to identify small molecule modulators of ERAD. Among the compounds screened, NCATS-SM0225 (referred to as 225) emerged as a potent ERAD inhibitor, but unexpectedly, it was found to bind to voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs). Binding of 225 to VDACs triggers IP3R-MCU-dependent disruption of calcium homeostasis, which subsequently activates a calcium-PERK-STIM1 signaling. This cascade leads to the degradation of key ERAD complex proteins (HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1) and selectively induces cancer cell death while sparing normal cells. These findings provide critical insights into ERAD biology, its interplay with calcium signaling, and its potential as a cancer therapeutic target. This work highlights the utility of small molecule modulators in probing ERAD function and towards developing first-in-class cancer-selective therapies.

---

## Results

High-content screening for small molecule modulators of ERAD
During ERAD, misfolded proteins are recognized and retained in the ER, where luminal chaperones and lectins facilitate their delivery to ERAD complexes for retrotranslocation to the cytosol1,6. This process is essential for ERAD, as it enables misfolded proteins to be ubiquitinated and subsequently degraded by the proteasome. We have previously developed the drGFP reporter assay to monitor the final step of retrotranslocation, the complete dislocation of substrate proteins from the ER into the cytosol, in live cells36. This assay utilizes split GFP37, which reconstitutes fluorescence upon successful dislocation in the presence of a proteasome inhibitor, which provides a direct, real-time readout of ERAD activity (Fig. 1a, and Supplementary Movies 1–3). The null Hong Kong variant of α−1-antitrypsin (NHK), an ER luminal misfolded protein, was selected as the ERAD substrate (NHK-drGFP) in the primary screen, where changes in GFP intensity were visualized and quantified to assess ERAD activity36. CD3δ, an ER membrane substrate, was used in the drGFP (CD3δ-drGFP) assay as a secondary screen to confirm primary hits. Enhanced substrate dislocation increases GFP fluorescence, while inhibition (e.g., NMS-873-ap97/VCP inhibitor, in Fig. 1a) suppresses it, making this a powerful tool for studying ERAD and identifying potential modulators.

We first miniaturized and optimized the drGFP assay in 1536-well format to enable high-throughput screening. Pilot screening indicated robust assay performance (Supplementary Fig. 1a) with reproducible dose-dependent inhibition observed for p97/VCP inhibitor NMS-873, known to inhibit dislocation (Fig. 1b). The optimized assay was used to perform a screen of 96,047 compounds, which exhibited a favorable signal window (Fig. 1c) and a robust mean Z’ factor of 0.59 (Supplementary Fig. 1b). The primary screen yielded 956 hits, comprised of approved drugs, bioactive tool compounds, and diversity-collection molecules (Fig. 1d, and Supplementary Fig. 1c). We focused on the 419 compounds that originated from the diversity collections and retested them at 11 concentrations spanning 37 nM to 38 μM. Sixty-six compounds were confirmed as inhibitors, using the criteria of AC50 < 20 μM and > 60% efficacy. The hits were then tested in a second model of ER dislocation, using a misfolded CD3δ-based drGFP, with 62 of the 66 compounds (94%) categorized as active using the same 20 μM and 60% inhibition criteria. The 62 compounds represented thirteen chemotypes. Following removal of acutely cytotoxic compounds (showing cytotoxicity after 4 h treatment) and compounds with covalent warheads, six compounds, representing six chemotypes, were prioritized for further analysis (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Figs. 1d, e).

We next tested the six potential dislocation inhibitors for their effects on the stability of ΔF508CFTR, a well-established ERAD substrate and the cystic fibrosis-causing protein38,39. Baby hamster kidney fibroblasts (BHK) stably expressing HA-ΔF508CFTR (HA-ΔF508CFTR-BHK cells)40,41 were treated with the putative inhibitors for 24 h. The results revealed that only 225 significantly increased the levels of HA-ΔF508CFTR in both the ER (core-glycosylated B form) and at the cell surface (fully glycosylated mature C form) (Fig. 1f). These increases are likely due to the inhibition of HA-ΔF508CFTR degradation, which promotes its forward trafficking (Fig. 1f). Notably, the non-glycosylated form of ΔF508CFTR (A form) was not observed in either control or 225-treated cells (Fig. 1f), suggesting that 225 affects the degradation and trafficking of the glycosylated forms of ΔF508CFTR40,41. Next, we resynthesized 225 (methods section) and tested the multiple batches in parallel. All the batches consistently showed reproducible activity in the dislocation assay (Supplementary Fig. 1f). To further validate and potentially improve the activity of 225, we designed and conducted a focused structure–activity relationship (SAR) study by synthesizing several structural analogs (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Note 1). Smaller substituents on the phenyl ring were generally tolerated and, in some cases, slightly improved potency (Supplementary Fig. 2; compounds 1-5). However, all other structural changes investigated (a subset which is included here) resulted in a significant loss of activity, including: the addition of alkyl groups in the benzylic position, N-alkylation of the sulfonamide, lactone-opening to various amides, truncation of the benzyl-sulfonamide altogether to parent amine, and changing sulfonamide to the analogous amide (Supplementary Fig. 2; compounds 6-10, respectively).

Validation of 225 as a dislocation inhibitor
Time-lapse imaging of the NHK-drGFP reporter showed that 225 inhibited dislocation as demonstrated by a dose-dependent reduction in drGFP, with an IC50 of 1.02 μM (Fig. 2a–c, and Supplementary Movies 4–7). Since inhibition of dislocation is expected to block ERAD, we further evaluated the effects of 225 on the degradation of NHK and an ER membrane substrate CD3δ, using cycloheximide (CHX) chase. Consistent with its role as a dislocation inhibitor, 225 significantly inhibited the degradation of both substrates (Fig. 2d–g). For ER luminal substrates, dislocation is a prerequisite for ubiquitination, as ubiquitination occurs on the cytosolic surface of the ER. As expected, 225 effectively inhibited NHK ubiquitination (Fig. 2h). These findings collectively establish 225 as a potent inhibitor of ERAD dislocation.

225 induces selective degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in HeLa cells
Inhibition of ERAD is expected to induce ER stress and activate the unfolded protein response (UPR). To explore the effects of 225 on UPR signaling and ERAD-related proteins in HeLa cells, we performed immunoblotting (IB) analyses, using tunicamycin (Tm) as a positive control for ER stress. Remarkably, treatment with 225 for 24-h resulted in a significant downregulation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1, accompanied by a phosphorylation-induced mobility shift of PERK (Fig. 3a), with the effects being both dose- and time-dependent. In addition, there was a modest downregulation of Sel1L protein (Fig. 3a). To determine whether the reduction in HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 levels was due to post-translational degradation, HeLa cells were treated with 225 alone or in combination with either the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib (BTZ) or the lysosome inhibitor chloroquine (CQ). All three proteins were stabilized by BTZ but not CQ (Supplementary Fig. 3a), indicating that 225 promotes their proteasomal degradation. Consistently, 225 did not decrease HERP1, OS9, or SEL1L mRNA; only FAM8A1 showed a modest reduction (Supplementary Fig. 3b).

Given that p97/VCP facilitates the extraction of ubiquitinated misfolded proteins from the ER for proteasomal degradation42, we investigated whether 225 targets HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 through the ERAD pathway. Treatment with p97/VCP inhibitors DBeQ and NMS-87343,44 effectively blocked the 225-induced degradation of all three proteins (Supplementary Fig. 3c), confirming their degradation via the ERAD-proteasome pathway. Consistent with these findings, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of transcriptome data from 225-treated HeLa cells revealed significant enrichment of UPR activation (Fig. 3b), which was further validated by IB (Fig. 3c). Notably, PERK signaling emerged as the most prominently activated pathway (Fig. 3b, d). Inhibition of PERK kinase activity partially rescued HeLa cell death induced by 225 (Fig. 3e). Together, these results demonstrate that 225 disrupts protein dislocation, induces the degradation of ERAD complex proteins, and activates PERK-mediated proapoptotic signaling.

225 selectively targets all three isoforms of VDAC (voltage-dependent anion channel)
To identify the molecular target of 225, a diazirine-based photoaffinity and clickable probe (225-cc, Supplementary Fig. 4c) was synthesized by incorporating 225 with a minimally interfering photo-affinity label (MI-PAL)45 to enable target identification studies (Fig. 4a, b). First, we confirmed that 225-cc retained dislocation inhibitory activity, with an IC50 of 9.8 μM in the NHK-drGFP assay (Supplementary Figs. 4a, b). Next, cells treated with 225-cc were irradiated with UV light (365 nm) to induce diazirine photolytic conversion into a reactive carbene, capable of covalent insertion into amino acid residues in close proximity. To identify 225-cc target proteins, a commercially available trifunctional probe, DdeTAMRA Biotin Azide, which contains a fluorescent dye and a chemically cleavable biotin pull-down handle (Supplementary Fig. 4c), was used to label 225-cc-bound proteins via copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC; ‘click’ reaction)46 (Supplementary Fig. 4d). The 225-cc-labeled proteins, now covalently bound to a fluorescent moiety, could be visualized on SDS-PAGE gels (Fig. 4a), and the biotin tag facilitated identification by mass spectrometry (MS) following affinity capture using streptavidin beads (Fig. 4b). These experiments indicated that 225-cc is quite selective, as a single protein band of approximately 35 kDa was observed in both total cell lysates and streptavidin pull down samples (Fig. 4a). MS analysis of the protein band pulled down by streptavidin beads revealed that the top three identified proteins were the three isoforms of VDAC, outer mitochondrial membrane proteins also localized in mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs)47,48 (Fig. 4b). Knockout of each VDAC isoform reduced 225 labeling to an extent consistent with the reported expression levels in HeLa cells49, with VDAC1 showing the most significant reduction (Fig. 4c). These results indicate that 225 binds to all three isoforms of VDAC.

The ER membrane protein complex (EMC) is an ER insertase, and recent reports suggest VDAC1 can associate with EMC via EMC3, EMC4, and EMC750. To further probe target specificity, we tested whether EMC mediates 225’s effects. Degradation of ERAD components (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1) persisted in 225-treated EMC3-, EMC4-, and EMC7-knockdown cells, similar to controls, and 225 did not affect the levels of these three EMC proteins (Supplementary Fig. 4e); EMC3 or EMC7 knockdown also did not alter 225-mediated dislocation inhibition in the drGFP assay (Supplementary Fig. 4f); and VDAC–EMC interactions were unchanged by 225 as demonstrated by VDAC1 co-IP with EMC3 or EMC4 (Supplementary Fig. 4g). These results do not support an EMC-dependent mechanism of 225 and further substantiate VDACs as the specific targets of 225.

As VDACs are not known to control ERAD but have been recently isolated as interacting proteins for SEL1L, a key cofactor for the HRD1 ERAD E3 ubiquitin ligase51, we next investigated the potential connection by knocking down each of the three VDAC isoforms and assessing the effects on NHK dislocation using NHK-drGFP reporter. Surprisingly, single knockdown of any VDAC isoform by itself markedly inhibited dislocation (Fig. 4d, e), supporting a role for VDACs in ERAD. Given the marked effects on dislocation, it was surprising that we succeeded in establishing viable VDAC KO cell lines (Fig. 4c), suggesting that a compensatory mechanism was activated to protect cells from the effects of dislocation inhibition. Since ER-phagy is a key compensatory response to ERAD inhibition9,52,53, we monitored ER-phagy activity using the well-established ss-RFP-GFP-KDEL reporter54 stably expressed in HeLa cells. Knockdown of each VDAC isoform activated ER-phagy, as indicated by a decrease in the GFP/RFP ratio (Fig. 4f) and the formation of RFP puncta accompanied (Fig. 4g). Similarly, knockdown of VDAC1 led to the relocalization of CD3δ-mCherry into puncta and a decrease in its cellular levels (Fig. 4h, i). These findings demonstrate that 225 selectively targets all three isoforms of VDAC and suggest that VDACs play a critical role in maintaining ERAD activity. The activation of ER-phagy following VDAC knockdown suggests that ER-phagy sequesters and degrades ERAD substrates, thereby reducing their dislocation from the ER.

225 directly interacts with VDAC1 and regulates its function in vitro
To validate the binding of 225 to the identified target proteins, we conducted microscale thermophoresis (MST) analysis. The equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) between 225 and recombinant human VDAC1 was determined to be 3.13 μM, indicating direct binding (Fig. 5a). To further examine 225 binding to VDACs in cells, we employed the Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA), which is based on the principle that ligand binding increases the thermal stability of its target protein, allowing detection of the stabilized protein in the soluble cellular fraction by immunoblotting or mass spectrometry55,56. Treatment with 225 increased the thermal stability of all three VDAC isoforms but not the control protein ATP5A (Fig. 5b). Together, these results provide strong evidence for a direct interaction between 225 and VDACs.

To examine if 225 binding to VDAC1 affects its channel function, we employed a voltage-clamp electrophysiology approach on a system of the recombinant human VDAC1 reconstituted into a planar lipid membrane57,58. This method allowed us to perform highly sensitive measurements of functional interaction between 225 and VDAC1 at the single-molecule level and to investigate the impact of 225 on VDAC1 basic properties, such as its single-channel conductance and voltage gating. The planar lipid membranes were formed from a mixture of dioleoyl-phosphatidylcholine (DOPC):dioleoyl-phosphatidylethanolamine (DOPE) (1:1 w/w), two major phospholipids of the mitochondrial outer membrane59,60, in symmetrical 1 M KCl buffer solution. Under these conditions, VDAC1 typically forms ion channels of ~4.0 nS conductance, which characteristically gate, i.e., transition from the high conducting “open” state to a variety of low conducting or “closed” states in response to the applied voltages61,62. In control, 225-free, experiments, the application of +/− 60 mV was required to observe consistent voltage gating (Fig. 5c). The addition of 225 at 200 nM and 400 nM concentrations resulted in VDAC1 gating at much lower amplitudes of negative potentials, specifically at −40 mV and −30 mV (indicated by arrows in Fig. 5c). This resulted in a 20–30 mV shift of the voltage required for gating of a single VDAC1 channel, compared to the control conditions (Fig. 5c). Thus, 225 promotes VDAC1 closure at reduced voltages in a concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 5c).

Quantification of voltage-gating and obtaining a 225 binding curve requires a statistical analysis of the gating of many channels. The multichannel experiments were performed under the application of slow triangular voltage waves (5 mHz, +/− 60 mV), which enable a slow channel closure and fast reopening, and allow us to collect responses of 50-100 channels to the applied voltages63,64. Figure 5d shows the normalized conductance-voltage plots at negative potentials (G/Gmax vs voltage), where G is the conductance at a given voltage and Gmax is the maximum conductance at voltages close to 0 mV. The multichannel measurements were performed under the same experimental conditions as single-channel measurements (Fig. 5c). The addition of 225 to the cis side of the membrane, enhanced VDAC1 gating by decreasing the minimum conductance (Gmin), calculated at |V| > 50 mV, in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 5d). Notably, the increased voltage-gating was observed in single- and multichannel experiments predominantly at potentials that are negative from the side of 225 addition, the cis side of the membrane. The gating response to 225 addition was quantified as normalized change in conductance, (Gmax - Gmin)/Gmin, and plotted versus 225 concentrations (Fig. 5e). These results point to a direct functional interaction between 225 and VDAC1. We can speculate that by promoting the VDAC1 closed state, 225 promotes calcium influx to mitochondria47,65, thus regulating calcium signaling through direct interaction with VDAC1.

225 induces calcium elevation in mitochondria, ER, and cytosol, leading to HERP1 and OS9 degradation
VDAC, the most abundant protein in the mitochondrial outer membrane, plays a critical role in regulating calcium influx, metabolism, and cell death47,66–69. To investigate the effects of 225 on intracellular calcium dynamics, we monitored calcium levels in mitochondria, cytosol, and ER using established fluorescent calcium sensors, including the cytosol calcium sensor GCaMP6F, the mitochondrial calcium sensor Mitycam, and the ER calcium sensor GCaMPer70. We observed that 225 induced a dose- and time-dependent increase in calcium levels across all three compartments (Fig. 6a–c). KO of individual VDAC isoforms or dual VDAC2/3 reduced 225-induced calcium elevation, while RNAi-mediated knockdown (KD) of VDAC1 in the context of VDAC2/3 KO (VDAC1KD/VDAC2-/-/VDAC3-/-) nearly abolished the effect of 225 on calcium levels across all compartments (Fig. 6d–f). Furthermore, VDACs were found to mediate 225-induced cell death, as measured by caspase-3/7 activation (Fig. 6g, h). Loss of all three VDAC isoforms significantly diminished 225-induced cell death (Fig. 6i), further supporting the conclusion that VDACs are the molecular targets through which 225 elevates intracellular calcium and triggers cell death. As a negative control, EMC knockdown did affect 225-induced increase in mitochondrial calcium (Supplementary Fig. 4h).

To determine whether calcium elevation mediates 225-induced cytotoxicity, we used the calcium chelator BAPTA-AM to sequester intracellular calcium during 225 treatment of HeLa cells. Calcium chelation completely abolished 225-induced cell death (Fig. 6j). Moreover, BAPTA-AM treatment prevented 225-induced degradation of HERP1 and OS9 (Fig. 6k). These findings suggest that 225 binds to VDACs, triggering a rise in intracellular calcium levels that subsequently induces the degradation of HERP1 and OS9 and ultimately leads to cell death.

Given reports that efsevin stabilizes the calcium-conductive state of VDAC71, we tested it alongside 225 in our ERAD assays. Under identical conditions, efsevin neither impaired dislocation nor reduced HERP1 or OS9 protein levels, whereas 225 robustly inhibited dislocation and decreased HERP1/OS9 (Supplementary Fig. 6a). These data indicate that efsevin does not inhibit ERAD in our system and support a mechanism for 225 that is distinct from efsevin.

225 preferentially targets a subgroup of cancer cells while sparing normal cells
To determine the potential cell type-dependent effects of 225, we randomly examined 16 different cancer cell lines derived from various cancers, including melanoma, glioma, breast cancer, liver cancer, pancreatic cancer, osteosarcoma, and mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Treatment with 225 induced the degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in 11 out of the 16 cancer cell lines while showing minimal or no effects in the remaining 5 cell lines (Fig. 7a). Notably, 225 had no impact on the protein levels of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in three types of primary normal human cells, including fibroblasts from three individuals, epidermal melanocytes, and hepatocytes (Fig. 7a). Importantly, the cytotoxicity of 225 showed a strong positive correlation with the degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1, with degradation-resistant cells showing limited cytotoxicity (Fig. 7a, b). The differential cytotoxicity of 225 was further validated by measuring caspase-3/7 activation (Supplementary Figs. 7a–d). Remarkably, the viability of normal cells was not impacted by 225 up to 10 μM concentrations that impacted cancer cells (Fig. 7b, Supplementary Fig. 7d) and concentrations up to 50 μM had no effect on primary human hepatocytes (Supplementary Fig. 7f). These results suggest that 225 selectively targets a subgroup of cancer cells while sparing normal cells, and this selectivity strongly correlates with its ability to induce the degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1.

To obtain proof-of-concept evidence for the antitumor efficacy of 225, we evaluated its activity in vivo using A375 melanoma xenografts, a 225-sensitive cancer model. Daily intraperitoneal administration of 225 (20 mg/kg) markedly inhibited tumor growth without detectable toxicity (Fig. 7c–e). Treated mice exhibited no clinical signs of adverse effects, and histological examination of the liver, pancreas, and kidney revealed no abnormalities (Supplementary Figs. 7g–i). Collectively, these results identify VDAC as a promising cancer-selective therapeutic target.

225-induced intracellular calcium elevation is a defining feature of its selective cytotoxicity
225 induces elevation of calcium in cytosol, mitochondria, and ER and causes death in HeLa cells (Fig. 6). Next, we examined whether this calcium elevation differentiates the selective cytotoxicity using 225-sensitive MCF7ca, A375, and A253 cells, and 225-insensitive MDA-MB-231, T47D, MDA-MD-453 cells, as well as primary human fibroblasts (HDFa, GM05294) as examples. Calcium increases were observed only in 225-sensitive cancer cells, with no significant changes observed in 225-insentitive cancer cells and primary human fibroblasts (Fig. 8a–c). These findings suggest that 225 preferentially targets a subgroup of cancer cells by disrupting calcium homeostasis and inducing the degradation of ERAD complex proteins, while sparing normal cells and a subgroup of cancer cells.

VDAC1 expression is frequently overexpressed in various cancers compared to normal cells and is associated with poor prognosis and tumor progression72,73. Next, we examined whether VDAC1 expression contributes to the differential sensitivity of 225. We found that VDAC1 protein levels are generally higher in sensitive cells and lower in insensitive or normal cells (Fig. 8d, e); however, one insensitive cell line (MDA-MB-231) expresses high levels of VDAC1 protein (Fig. 8d, e). Although the underlying mechanism that confer resistance of MDA-MB-231 to 225 are not understood, we speculate that mutations may alter downstream death-signaling pathways. We also analyzed mRNA expression data from the Human Protein Atlas74,75 and found no correlation between VDAC1 transcript abundance and protein levels (Fig. 8d-e vs. Supplementary Fig. 8a). This suggests that steady-state VDAC1 protein abundance is regulated by translational efficiency or protein stability rather than transcription. Consistent with this possibility, treatment of HeLa cells (a sensitive line) with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib markedly stabilized VDAC proteins (Supplementary Fig. 8b), indicating that VDACs are an unstable protein subject to proteasomal degradation, thereby affecting their steady-state protein levels. Taken together, these new findings suggest that VDAC1 protein abundance may contribute to the differential sensitivity to 225.

Calcium influx and IP3R activity mediate 225-induced intracellular calcium elevation and cell death
The 225-induced increase in intracellular calcium is likely driven by calcium influx from the extracellular space. This was confirmed by the failure of 225 to elevate intracellular calcium when HeLa cells were cultured in calcium-free medium (Fig. 9a–c). The simultaneous increase in calcium levels across the ER, mitochondria, and cytosol suggests that 225 broadly disrupts calcium homeostasis following VDAC binding. One potential mediator of these effects is the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R), as IP3R, grp75, and VDAC form a complex at mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs) that facilitates calcium transport from the ER to mitochondria76. To test this hypothesis, cells were treated with the IP3R inhibitor 2-APB77. 2-APB effectively inhibited 225-induced calcium increases in all three subcellular compartments and reduced cytotoxicity (Fig. 9d, e), implicating IP3R as a mediator of changes in calcium homeostasis. Furthermore, 2-APB also blocked 225-induced PERK activation and the degradation of HERP1 and OS9 (Fig. 9f). Coimmunoprecipitation experiments revealed that 225 significantly enhances the interaction between VDAC1 and IP3R in calcium-dependent manner (Fig. 9g, h), consistent with 225 altering complexes at the MAMs that control calcium. Inhibiting the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU), which is specifically responsible for the uptake of calcium into the mitochondrial matrix78, also diminished the cytotoxicity of 225 (Fig. 9i). These findings suggest that 225 binding to VDAC1 enhances the VDAC1-IP3R interaction, facilitates a rise in calcium levels across intracellular compartments, activates PERK, and triggers degradation of ERAD complex proteins, which ultimately culminates in cell death.

STIM1 regulates 225-induced calcium influx, and its phosphorylation mediates 225-induced ERAD complex degradation and cell death
The observations that 225-induced intracellular calcium dynamic changes require (1) extracellular calcium influx (Figs. 9a–c) and (2) ER contributions, mediated by IP3R (Fig. 9d, e), led us to hypothesize that STIM1, a key regulator of store-operated calcium entry (SOCE), might contribute to these events79,80. To investigate this possibility, we knocked down STIM1 and measured its effects on intracellular calcium levels. STIM1 knockdown disrupted cellular calcium homeostasis, as reflected by increased calcium levels in the ER, cytosol, and mitochondria to varying degrees (Fig. 10a). Notably, 225 failed to further elevate calcium levels in STIM1-KD cells (Fig. 10b), suggesting that STIM1 regulates 225-induced calcium elevation.

While elevated calcium is generally toxic to cells, STIM1 knockdown unexpectedly diminished 225-induced cytotoxicity and reduced PERK expression (Fig. 10c, d). This result is consistent with experiments identifying PERK as a crucial mediator of 225-induced cell death (Fig. 3e). Coimmunoprecipitation experiments revealed that STIM1 interacts with PERK, and 225 enhanced this interaction (Fig. 10e). Given that PERK is activated by 225, we investigated whether PERK phosphorylates STIM1. Indeed, 225 induced a mobility shift in STIM1, and the Phos-Tag assay confirmed that this shift was due to phosphorylation (Fig. 10f, g). The 225-induced phosphorylation of STIM1 was inhibited by the PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (Fig. 10f). Furthermore, PERK inhibition, like STIM1 knockdown, diminished 225-induced degradation of HERP1 and OS9 (Fig. 10f). Consistently, PERK knockdown reduced 225-induced inhibition of NHK dislocation (Fig. 10h, i). These findings indicate that 225 activates PERK, which phosphorylates STIM1, resulting in the degradation of HERP1 and OS9 and inhibition of ERAD.

STIM1 and PERK have not been previously reported to interact with VDAC1. To determine how 225 binding to VDAC1 could affect their association, we measured potential interactions among these proteins using co-immunoprecipitation (coIP). VDAC1 was found to interact with STIM1 and PERK in addition to IP3R (Fig. 10j). Interestingly, treatment with 225 enhanced the VDAC1–IP3R interaction but reduced its association with STIM1 and PERK (Fig. 10j). Concomitantly, 225 increased STIM1–PERK complex formation, which was dependent on calcium but independent of PERK kinase activity (Fig. 10k, l). These results suggest that 225 binding to VDAC1 elevates intracellular calcium levels, thereby remodeling the interaction network among VDAC1, IP3R, STIM1, and PERK. The increased VDAC1–IP3R interaction further amplifies calcium influx, while enhanced PERK–STIM1 association and PERK-mediated STIM1 phosphorylation destabilize HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1. Collectively, these events coincide with sustained calcium elevation, culminating in cell death (see model in Figur S9).

## Methods

Cell culture
HeLa (CCL-2), HepG2 (HB-8065), A-375 (CRL-1619), U-2OS (HTB-96), A253 (HTB-41), PSN1 (CRL-3211), Primary Dermal Fibroblast (HDFa, PCS-201-012) and Primary Epidermal Melanocyte (HEMa, PCS-200-013) cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, USA). U-251MG (09063001) and U-87MG (89081402) were obtained from Millipore Sigma. Normal untransformed fibroblast GM05294 and GM04390 cell lines were purchased from Coriell Institute. MDA-MB-231 (CRM-HTB-26), MDA-MB-453 (HTB-131), SK-BR-3 (HTB-30), BT474 (HTB-20), T-47D (HTB-133), and MIAPaCa-2 (CRL-1420) cell lines were obtained from Dr. Mark J. Henderson (NCATS/NIH). MCF7ca (MCF7 human breast cancer cell lines transfected with aromatase gene) cells were obtained from Dr. Yun Qiu (University of Maryland, Baltimore). Hepatocyte and Huh7 cells were obtained from Dr. Hongbing Wang (University of Maryland, Baltimore). HeLa cells stably expressing SP-S11-NHK-HA and S1-10 were established previously36.

All cell lines were maintained at 37°C in a 5% CO₂ humidified incubator. GM05294 and GM04390 were cultured in Minimum Essential Medium (MEM). HDFa was maintained in Fibroblast Basal Medium (ATCC® PCS-201-030™) supplemented with Fibroblast Growth Kit-Serum-free (ATCC® PCS-201-040™), HEMa is maintained in Dermal Cell Basal Medium (ATCC PCS-200-030) supplemented with Adult Melanocyte Growth Kit (ATCC PCS-200-042). PSN1 and T-47D were cultured in RPMI-1640 Medium. MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-453 were cultured in Leibovitz’s L-15 Medium. Other cell lines were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM). All normal cell lines were supplemented with 15% fetal bovine serum and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin. All cancer cell lines were supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin. For calcium-free conditions, cells were incubated in calcium-free DMEM (21068028, Invitrogen).

Generation of plasmid constructs
