The ssRFP-GFP-KEDL insert was excised using the EcoRI restriction site and ligated into the pLVX-EF1α-IRES-Puro vector (Takara Bio), which was digested with the same enzyme. Related primers are listed in Supplementary Table 1 in Extended data. All expression constructs were verified by DNA sequencing.

Dislocation-induced reconstituted GFP (drGFP) assay
HeLa cells stably expressing SP-S11-NHK-HA and S1-10 (NHK-drGFP)36 were plated in 96-well plates (2×10⁴ cells/well) and cultured overnight. After replacing the medium, cells were treated with indicated concentrations of 225 and/or BTZ (2 μM). GFP fluorescence was monitored in real-time using a 20× objective on the IncuCyte S3 live-cell analysis system.

drGFP-based high-content screening
Primary screening. To identify small molecule modulators of ER dislocation, NHK-drGFP reporter-expressing HeLa cells were seeded in black low base 1536-well assay plates (EBA141000A; Aurora) at a density of ~1000 cells per well in 5 μL of Fluorobrite DMEM media (A18967-01; Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS (SH30071.03, Cytivia), 5 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin (10378-016; Gibco), 21 mM HEPES (15630-080; Gibco) and 2 mM Glutamine (25030-081; Gibco) using a Multidrop Combi reagent dispenser (5840330; Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a small tube metal tip dispensing cassette (24073295; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Plates were cultured overnight (16 h) in incubators maintained at 37°C, with 5% CO2, and 95% humidity prior to the addition of 20 nL compound (dissolved in DMSO) using a Kalypsys pintool equipped with a 1536-pin array. To monitor ER dislocation, cells were incubated for 15 minutes, then treated with 2 μL of media containing 21 μM (6 μM final) Bortezomib (S1013; SelleckChem) to promote the accumulation of NHK-drGFP following the addition of compound. Plates were then incubated for 4 h prior to GFP quantification using an Acumen EX3 Microplate Cytometer (TTPLabtech). Data was normalized to multiple replicates (n=32) of cells treated with and without bortezomib, plus an equivalent volume of DMSO. To monitor assay performance, each plate included a 16 pt titration of the p97 inhibitor, NMS-873 (HY-15713; MedChemExpress), as a reference control. Library compounds demonstrating significant reduction of GFP signal (≤60% activity relative to DMSO) were replated in 11 pt titration and re-tested, as described, to confirm inhibitory activity, generate dose-response curves and calculate AC50 values.

Secondary Assay. Compounds confirmed in dose-response follow-up testing and exhibiting select hit parameters (≤60% activity relative to DMSO controls and AC50 ≤25 μM) were then re-tested in a secondary assay employing the same stable cell line. Briefly, cells were seeded at ~1000 cells per well in ultra-low base 1536-well, 188 μM film-bottom assay plates (EBC241000A; Aurora) and treated with compound and bortezomib, as described. Following 3.75 h of incubation, each well received 1 μL of pre-warmed media containing 25 ng/mL (3.125 ng/mL final) Hoechst (H3570; Invitrogen) using a Multidrop Combi reagent dispenser (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Plates were pulse centrifuged (30 s at 1000 rpm) using a benchtop centrifuge (5804R; Eppendorf) equipped with a microplate rotor and bucket (Eppendorf; EP-2DWPAT) then incubated 15 min at room temperature prior to quantification using an InCell Analyzer 2000 Imaging Plate Reader System or Opera Phenix Plus High-Content Screening System. Acquired images were processed using a Columbus Image Data Storage and Analysis System to quantify cellular GFP based on nuclear staining and corrected for background. Data was normalized to multiple replicates (n=32) of cells treated with and without bortezomib, plus an equivalent volume of DMSO. To monitor assay performance, each plate included a 16 pt titration of the p97 inhibitor, NMS-873, as a reference control.

Establishment of gene-modified cell lines
ssRFP-GFP-KDEL stable cell line. HeLa cells were transfected with pLVX-ssRFP-GFP-KDEL plasmid using Lipofectamine 3000 (L3000015, Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s protocol. After 48 h, stable transfectants were selected with puromycin. Positive clones were maintained under puromycin selection and verified by fluorescence microscopy and Western blot analysis.

VDAC knockout cell lines. VDAC1, VDAC2, VDAC3, and VDAC2/VDAC3 knockout HeLa cell lines were generated using CRISPR-Cas9. Single-guide RNA expression plasmids (Addgene) targeting each VDAC isoform were transfected into HeLa cells cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS. Transfected cells were selected with puromycin (2 μg/mL) for 3 days. Successful knockout was confirmed by immunoblotting using isoform-specific anti-VDAC antibodies. (Primer sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 1.)

siRNA Knockdown. Negative Control siRNA was purchased from Ambion. PERK siRNA (9024S) was purchased from Cell Signaling Technology. All other siRNAs were synthesized by Millipore Sigma (Supplementary Table 2). All siRNAs were transfected with Lipofectamine® RNAiMAX transfection reagent (Invitrogen) using siRNA in Opti-MEM with no antibiotic. After 72 h of transfection, knockdown efficiency was confirmed by western blotting. Cells were then treated with 225, and downstream effects were assessed.

Cytoheximide (CHX) chase35. To measure the degradation rate and stability of NHK and CD3δ35, HeLa cells stably expressing HA-tagged NHK or CD3δ were plated and allowed to reach 70−80% confluence before initiating the chase experiment. CHX was added to the culture medium at a final concentration of 50 μg/mL to halt de novo protein synthesis. Cells were incubated with either CHX alone or along with 225 for the indicated time points. Then cells were harvested and processed for immunoblotting with anti-HA and anti-β-actin antibodies.

Immunoprecipitation (IP). Cells transfected with indicated plasmids or empty vector were treated with DMSO (control) or 225 for 3 h, then lysed in buffer (150 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris/HCl pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.2% NP-40) containing protease inhibitors. For each IP reaction, 700 μg of protein in 800 μL total volume was used. Lysates from cells expressing ectopic proteins were incubated with anti-GFP or anti-HA affinity beads for 2 h at 4°C with gentle shaking. Beads were washed three times with 700 μL lysis buffer before processing for immunoblotting (IB).

NHK ubiquitination was analyzed by re-immunoprecipitation (Re-IP)35. Briefly, HeLa cells expressing NHK-HA were treated with BTZ (2 μM) with or without 2 μM 225. Cells were then collected and lysed in (150 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris/HCl pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.2% NP-40) containing protease inhibitors, and NHK-HA was immunoprecipitated using an anti-HA affinity matrix. To eliminate non-specifically bound proteins, immunoprecipitates were denatured with 2% SDS, and beads were removed by centrifugation. The supernatants were diluted 20-fold in native lysis buffer, and NHK-HA was re-immunoprecipitated before immunoblotting for HA and ubiquitin.

Immunoblotting (IB). Total cell lysates were prepared in lysis buffer (10 mM Tris/HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.2% NP-40, 0.5% Triton X-100, pH 7.5) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking nonspecific binding sites with 5% milk for 1 h at room temperature, membranes were probed with primary antibodies, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Following TBST washes, immunoreactive bands were detected using SuperSignal West Pico PLUS or Femto Maximum Sensitivity chemiluminescent substrates.

Caspase-3/7 activity assay. Apoptosis was assessed using the IncuCyte® Caspase-3/7 Green Apoptosis Assay. HeLa cells were treated with 225 at the indicated concentrations in the presence of the caspase-3/7 reagent (1:2000 dilution). Fluorescence intensity, reflecting caspase-3/7 activity, was measured in real-time using the IncuCyte® S3 system.

Target identification using photoaffinity and clickable 225 and Mass Spectrometry (MS). Cells were cultured to ~80% confluence and incubated with 5 μM of 225-cc in the presence or absence of 80 μM 225 for 30 min at 37°C to allow compound binding to target proteins. After incubation, cells were rinsed with PBS and irradiated with UV light (355 nm) for 20 minutes on ice to covalently crosslink probe 225-cc to its interacting proteins. Following crosslinking, cells were washed with cold PBS and lysed in 1% NP40 buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 10% Glycerol, 1% NP40) containing EDTA free protease inhibitor cocktail. The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C, and protein concentration was determined. Urea was then added to cleared lysate (~680 mg urea to 1 mL lysate) to achieve a final urea concentration of approximately 8 M.

For pull-down assay, 1.3 mL of the urea-denatured lysate (~1.5 mg proteins) was mixed with the following reagents: 30 μL of 1 mM Dde-TAMRA-Biotin-Azide (Click Chemistry Tools, 1367-1), 70 μL of 100 mM THPTA, 14 μL of 100 mM CuSO4 and 70 μL of 300 mM sodium ascorbate. The click reaction mixture was incubated for 30 min at room temperature in the dark on a rotator. Following incubation, proteins were precipitated by cold methanol and chloroform. Precipitated proteins were resuspended in 1% SDS, 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), and 150 mM NaCl, followed by sonication. Each sample was incubated with 50 μL Pierce™ Streptavidin Magnetic Beads (Thermo Fisher, 88816) for 1.5 h at room temperature. Beads were washed three times with the same resuspension buffer. After washing, beads were boiled in SDS loading buffer containing 5 mM biotin and proceeded to SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting if applicable. For mass spectrometry analysis, fluorescent bands at ~35 kDa (both 225-cc and with competition control by adding free 225) and ~18 kDa (only 225-cc) were excised (3 gel pieces in total, N=1 for each condition) and cut into 1 mm pieces. Gel pieces were washed twice with 50% methanol for 10 minutes each, then the gel pieces were stored at −20°C prior to LC-MS/MS analysis. The click reaction can be scale down to 50 μL total volume with 50 μg proteins when the sample is only used for fluorescent visualization of the probe-labeled proteins in the SDS-PAGE gel.

For gel band excision, clean and sterile razors were used to cut the desired band/slice in a process-protection hood. The slice was further cut into 1×1 mm pieces prior to de-staining, reduction and alkylation, tryptic digestion and peptide extraction81. In brief, 1×1 mm gel pieces were transferred into pre-rinsed 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes and re-swelled in 50 µL of 20 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC), followed by dehydration with 50 µL of acetonitrile. After discarding the solvent, the gel pieces were re-swelled in 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) and incubated for 1 h at 56°C for reduction, followed by alkylation with 55 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for 45 min at room temperature in the dark. The solution was discarded, and the gel pieces were washed with 50 mM ABC and dehydrated again with acetonitrile. After the final dehydration step, the gels were dried completely using a SpeedVac. The dried gel pieces were then re-swelled on ice for 45–60 min in 25 µL of 10 ng/µL trypsin prepared in 20 mM ABC. Excess trypsin solution was removed, and the gel pieces were covered with 25 µL of 20 mM ABC and incubated overnight at 37°C for digestion. Peptides were extracted once with 25 µL of 20 mM ABC and three times with 50 µL of 50% acetonitrile containing 5% formic acid. All supernatants were combined and lyophilized by speed-vac and resuspended in 2% acetonitrile, 97.9% water, and 0.1% formic acid buffer for liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis. The LC-MS/MS analysis of in-gel digested product was performed using an UltiMate 3000-nano LC system coupled to the Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer equipped with the Nanospray Flex ion source (Thermo Fisher). Peptides were loaded onto the trap column (Acclaim PepMap 100 C18, 75 μm × 2 cm, particle size: 3 μm, 100 Å; Thermo Fisher) by autosampler using loading solvent (2% acetonitrile in MS-grade water, 0.1% FA) at a flow rate of 4 μL/min. Elution of peptides from the analytical column (with spray tip, 75 μm × 20 cm, 1.7 μm, 100 Å; CoAnn Technologies) was performed using a 60 min method (~45 min gradient) starting at 98% solution A (0.1% formic acid in MS-grade water) at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The mobile phase was maintained at 2% solution B (80% acetonitrile, 19.9% water, 0.1% formic acid) for 5 min, 2–9% B for 2 min, 9–38% B for 33 min, 38–50% B for 2 min, 50–90% B for 3 min, and maintained at 90% B for 6 min, followed by re-equilibration of the column with 2% B for 7 min. Column oven temperature was set as 40°C. The mass spectrometer was operated in positive-ionization mode with spray voltage set at 1800 V, and ion transfer tube temperature set at 250°C. The MS scan was operated at data-dependent acquisition mode, with full MS scans over a mass range of m/z 375–1800 with detection in the Orbitrap (120K resolution) and with auto gain control (AGC) set to 1.0×106. The fragment ion spectra were acquired in Orbitrap (15K resolution) with a normalized collision energy of 28% at HCD activation mode. In each cycle of data-dependent acquisition analysis, the most intense ions were selected for the MS/MS analysis, and the cycle time for MS and MS/MS analysis was set as 2 s. The AGC for MS/MS was set as 5.0×104 and the maximum injection time was 22 ms. Precursor ions with charges of +2 to +7 were isolated for MS/MS sequencing. The MS/MS isolation window was 1.2 Da, and the dynamic exclusion time was set at 60 s with a mass tolerance of ±10 ppm.

Proteome Discoverer software suite (version 3.0, Thermo Fisher) with Sequest algorithm was used for peptide identification. The MS raw data were searched against a Swiss-Prot human database (version November 2022, reviewed database) consisting of 20,328 entries using the following parameters: precursor ion mass tolerance of 10 ppm and a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.02 Da. Peptides were searched using fully tryptic cleavage constraints and up to two internal cleavage sites were allowed for tryptic digestion. Fixed modifications consisted of carbamidomethylation of cysteine. Variable modifications considered were oxidation of methionine residues. Peptide identification false discovery rates (FDR) were limited to a maximum of 0.01 using identifications from a concatenated database from the non-decoy and the decoy databases. Minimum number of peptide for protein identification was set as 1 and protein was ranked by number of PSMs.

Differential expression and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)82. Differential expression analysis between 225-treated and untreated samples (three biological replicates per group) was first performed using the DESeq2 R package (v1.14.1), which models digital gene expression data with a negative binomial distribution. Genes with a p value < 0.05 were designated as differentially expressed and were subsequently ranked based on their expression changes to serve as input for gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). GSEA was then performed using the GSEA software (v4.4.0, available at http://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp) with default parameters to identify biological pathways and transcriptional programs regulated by compound 225. Pre-defined gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB), including the Hallmark and KEGG collections, were evaluated, and pathways with a false discovery rate (FDR)–adjusted p-value < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched. The normalized enrichment score (NES) was used to quantify the degree of enrichment for each gene set82.

Microscale thermophoresis (MST). Recombinant human VDAC1 bearing an N-terminal His-tag (Proteogenix, Cat#: ARO-P13933) was equilibrated on ice for 1 h in PBS (pH 7.4) supplemented with 0.05% n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM). His-tag–directed fluorescent labeling was performed using the RED-tris-NTA 2nd Generation dye (NanoTemper, Cat#: MO-L018) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The high-affinity interaction between His-tags and tris-NTA (~1–10 nM) ensured selective labeling without additional purification. To determine the binding affinity of compound 225 for VDAC1, a two-fold serial dilution of 225 was prepared in PBS containing 0.05% DDM, starting at 100 µM to generate a twelve-point titration series. Fluorescently labeled protein (10 µL, final concentration 50 nM) was mixed with 10 µL of each 225 concentration, resulting in a maximal compound concentration of 50 µM. Samples were incubated for 30 min at room temperature and loaded into Monolith Premium Capillaries (NanoTemper, Cat#: MO-K025). Two independent replicate measurements were collected for each concentration.

MST measurements were acquired using a Monolith X instrument (NanoTemper Technologies GmbH) with high IR-laser power and automatic excitation settings. MST response values were automatically converted to “fraction bound” in MO. Control software (v2.7.1). Duplicate measurements at each concentration were averaged, and the averaged values were used to generate the binding curve. The dissociation constant (Kd) was determined by nonlinear regression using the MO. Control software.

Cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA)55,56. CETSA was employed to evaluate compound–protein engagement in cells55,56. HeLa cells were seeded and allowed to adhere, then treated with 2 μM compound 225 or an equivalent volume of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) at 37°C for 1 h. After treatment, cells were harvested by scraping and lysed in buffer (150 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris/HCl pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.4% NP-40) supplemented with protease inhibitors. The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000 × g for 10 min, and protein concentrations of the resulting supernatants were determined and normalized across samples. Normalized aliquots of the lysates were heated at the indicated temperatures for 3 min, followed by cooling to room temperature (25°C) for 3 min. The samples were then centrifuged at 20,000 × g for 20 min to separate soluble proteins from precipitated aggregates. Soluble fractions were mixed with 4× SDS sample buffer and subjected to immunoblotting.

VDAC1 gating. Planar lipid bilayers were made by the apposition of two monolayers comprised of the 1:1 (w:w) mixture of 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC) and 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (DOPE) lipids (Avanti Polar Lipids, Alabaster, AL) dissolved in pentane. These monolayers were formed across a ∼125 μm (in multichannel experiments) and 75 μm (in single channel experiments) diameter aperture within a 15-μm-thick Teflon film separating two ∼1.5-mL compartments filled with 1 M KCl solution buffered by 5 mM HEPES at pH 7.4, as previously described64. The recombinant human VDAC1 was a generous gift of Tsyr-Yan Dharma Yu (Institute of Atomic and Molecular Sciences, Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan). VDAC1 channel insertion was obtained after addition of 0.2–0.5 μl of VDAC1 diluted in 100 mM Tris, 50 mM KCl, 1 mM EDTA, 15% (v/v) DMSO, 2.5% (v/v) Triton X-100, pH 7.35 to the cis compartment of the experimental chamber while stirring. The procedure of VDAC reconstitution into lipid bilayers was described previously64,83. Potential is defined as positive when it is greater on the cis side, the side of compound 225 and VDAC1 addition.

Ion current recordings were acquired using an Axopatch 200B amplifier (Axon Instruments) in voltage clamp mode, following previously reported protocols83. Current signals were filtered at 10 kHz with a low-pass Bessel filter, digitized at a sampling frequency of 50 kHz, and analyzed using pClamp 10.7 software (Axon Instruments). For single-channel analyses in Clampfit 10.7, recordings were further digitally filtered with a 5 kHz 8-pole Bessel low-pass filter.

Voltage-dependence of VDAC gating was analyzed using a previously described protocol63,64 under the application of a slow, symmetric triangular voltage wave (±60 mV, 5 mHz) generated by an Arbitrary Waveform Generator 33220A (Agilent Technologies). Data were sampled at 2 Hz frequency and analyzed as detailed earlier63 using a custom in-house algorithm and pClamp 10.7 software. In each experiment, current records were collected from membranes containing 10-50 channels in response to 5–10 periods of voltage waves to ensure data collection from more than 50 channels per experiment. Only the part of the wave, during which the channels were reopening, was used for the subsequent analysis for the reasons described elsewhere63.

Xenograft. The A375 human melanoma cell line was maintained in high-glucose DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. Compound 225 was formulated in a vehicle consisting of N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, polyethyleneglycol 300, propylene glycol, and 20% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin. Male BALB/c-nu mice (7 weeks old) were housed in a specific pathogen-free facility under standard conditions. We fully acknowledge the journal’s policy on sex inclusion and recognize the importance of sex as a biological variable. In our initial in vivo proof-of-principle study, only male BALB/c-nu mice were used to minimize biological variability and obtain clear efficacy data. ### Reviewer 4

Key Results
This manuscript identifies a novel small molecule, NCATS-SM0225 (“225”), as a selective ERAD inhibitor that binds to
voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs). Through a combination of high-content screening, biochemical validation, and
mechanistic dissection, the authors suggest that 225 triggers an intracellular calcium imbalance via a VDAC-IP3R-PERK-
STIM1 signaling axis. This leads to the degradation of ERAD complex components (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1) and induces
cell death selectively in cancer cells while sparing normal cells. The work uncovers a previously unrecognized role for
VDACs in ERAD regulation and presents a compelling chemical probe for further study of ER proteostasis and cancer-
selective cytotoxicity.
Validity
The data are of high quality, robust, and generally well-controlled. The experimental workflow is thorough, including
orthogonal validation of dislocation inhibition (GFP reporters, CHX chase, ubiquitination assays), target identification
(photoaffinity labeling and MS), and functional studies using gene knockouts and chemical inhibitors. However, the precise
mechanism of 225 binding to VDACs and how this affects VDAC function at a structural level remains speculative. The
authors acknowledge this and propose it as future work.
Significance
The identification of a VDAC-targeting small molecule that selectively disrupts ERAD and kills cancer cells is novel and
potentially impactful. This work opens new avenues in cancer biology, proteostasis, and chemical biology. It also proposes
an alternative strategy to targeting UPR sensors directly — by modulating ERAD upstream. The selective toxicity of 225 to
certain cancer cell lines suggests translational relevance. While the mechanistic basis of this selectivity is not fully resolved,
the dataset lays a solid foundation for follow-up studies.
Data and Methodology
The methodology is state-of-the-art and spans a wide range of experimental techniques, including high-content screening,
SAR chemistry, CRISPR knockouts, calcium imaging, and GSEA transcriptomic profiling. The description of materials and
methods is detailed and transparent. Use of the drGFP reporter for dislocation, combined with dose-responses, time
courses, and structure–activity relationships, makes the data solid. Photoaffinity labeling with mass spectrometry is well
executed, and VDAC target identification is convincing. If available, raw calcium traces or proteomics data could be made
public in supplementary datasets.
Analytical Approach
Quantitative results are consistently supported by replicates, appropriate statistical tests, and careful normalization. The use
of dose-response curves, IC50 values, and multiple replicates is appropriate. GSEA is correctly applied and complements
the mechanistic data. The authors have been transparent about sample sizes and statistical significance thresholds.
Suggested Improvements
The authors present a compelling study identifying VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as direct binding partners of compound
225. They propose that 225 perturbs calcium homeostasis at the ER-mitochondria interface via these outer mitochondrial
membrane proteins, thereby inhibiting ER-associated degradation (ERAD), activating the unfolded protein response (UPR),
and triggering apoptosis. While the data are generally sound and well-presented, I believe an alternative, structurally
grounded interpretation offers a more parsimonious explanation of the experimental findings.
Recent structural studies (Li et al., Aging 2023, DOI:10.18632/aging.205660) demonstrate that VDAC1 directly binds the ER
membrane protein complex (EMC) at ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs), locking the EMC in a non-insertase
conformation.
Earlier proteomic mapping
(Christianson, J., Olzmann, J., Shaler, T. et al. Defining human ERAD networks through an integrative mapping strategy. Nat
Cell Biol 14, 93–105 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1038/ncb2383)
showed that multiple EMC subunits interact with Derlin-1 and Derlin-2, core components of the ERAD dislocation
machinery. This raises the possibility that compound 225 inhibits ERAD not by modulating VDAC channel activity directly,
but by stabilizing a non-functional EMC–VDAC complex that disrupts EMC-dependent membrane insertion of ERAD
components such as Derlin-1.
Below, I analyze the major data types presented by the authors in support of their model and offer the alternative EMC-
mediated interpretation.
1. Identification of VDAC1/2/3 as targets of 225:
The authors used a clickable photoaffinity analog of 225 to identify VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as binding targets.
This result is compatible with both their interpretation (VDAC as a functional target for calcium flux regulation) and my alternative
model (VDACs as structural partners of EMC, mediating 225 activity via this complex).
2. Inhibition of ERAD and activation of UPR by 225:
225 blocks degradation of NHK and HA-DeltaF508CFTR, canonical ERAD substrates. It also induces expression of BiP,
CHOP, and ATF4. The authors ascribe this to ER calcium dysregulation. However, a simpler model is that 225-bound
VDAC stabilizes EMC in a non-insertase state, blocking the membrane integration of Derlin-1 and other EMC-dependent
ERAD components, thereby directly impairing ERAD and triggering proteostatic stress. This hypothesis explains all
observed consequences (ERAD block, UPR, cell death) without invoking a poorly defined Ca2+ channeling role for VDACs.
3. Triple VDAC1 KD / VDAC2⁻/⁻ / VDAC3⁻/⁻ cells resist 225 phenotypes:
The authors interpret this as evidence that VDACs are the functional conduits for calcium flux perturbed by 225.
However, in the alternative model, the absence of VDACs prevents 225 from stabilizing the EMC–VDAC complex. This
restores EMC function and Derlin-1 insertion, preserving ERAD and preventing downstream UPR and Ca2+
dysregulation. Thus, the triple KO phenotype is compatible with both models.
4. ER calcium flux and 225-induced cell death:
Calcium flux is clearly altered by 225, but the authors do not provide direct electrophysiological or structural evidence that
225 opens or blocks VDAC pores. Given that VDAC is primarily known as a metabolite channel in the outer mitochondrial
membrane, and that Ca2+ flow between ER and mitochondria typically involves IP3R-GRP75-VDAC tethers, it remains
uncertain whether VDAC alone mediates Ca2+ leak. In contrast, the EMC-centered model predicts that ER stress and UPR
activation are primary, and that calcium dysregulation is a downstream effect of ER proteostasis failure.
Conclusion:
In light of published structural and proteomic data, the model in which compound 225 exerts its effects by stabilizing a non-
insertase EMC–VDAC complex provides a mechanistically unified explanation of all observed phenotypes: ERAD
inhibition, UPR activation, and calcium flux. It avoids invoking a direct gating effect of 225 on VDACs, for which no structural
or biophysical support is currently provided. I suggest the authors consider this alternative mechanism in the discussion and
test whether EMC activity or Derlin-1 insertion is altered upon 225 treatment.
This model is not incompatible with the authors' data, but may better contextualize the role of VDACs as structural, rather
than purely channel, components at MAMs. It also makes distinct predictions about EMC dependency that could be
experimentally tested.
Suggested experiments:
Assess Derlin-1 levels and membrane insertion after 225 treatment
Test EMC–VDAC complex stability or conformation changes in the presence of 225
Compare 225 sensitivity in cells with EMC subunit knockdown or mutation
Clarity and Context
The manuscript is clearly written and accessible. Figures are well designed and support the main conclusions. The
discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within existing literature and discusses limitations transparently. The
novelty of VDACs in ERAD is well supported.
References
The referencing is thorough and appropriate. Key prior work on ERAD, UPR, VDAC function, and chemical screening is
cited. I did not note any major omissions.
Your Expertise
My expertise includes ER proteostasis and chemical biology. I am confident in assessing the main findings and mechanistic
claims. I did not independently evaluate the full MS data or chemical synthesis protocols but found the presented validation
to be sufficient.

compensatory Ca2+ influx, resulting in elevation of both ER and cytosolic Ca2+.
2) Complex remodeling requires Ca2+: Our data showed that under basal conditions, VDAC1 co-
immunoprecipitates with STIM1, PERK, and IP3R (Fig. 10j). Upon 225 treatment, VDAC1– IP3R
interaction increased, whereas VDAC1–STIM1 and VDAC1–PERK associations decreased (Fig.
10j), coinciding with enhanced PERK–STIM1 interaction (Figs. 10e, 10k). Notably, the 225-
induced increases in VDAC1–IP3R and PERK–STIM1 interactions were abolished by Ca2+
chelation (Figs. 9h, 10k). Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of PERK did not prevent the
225-induced PERK–STIM1 interaction (Fig. 10l), indicating that elevated intracellular Ca2+,
rather than PERK catalytic activity, drives the enhanced PERK–STIM1 association.
Working model: Under resting conditions, a PERK–STIM1 complex associates with VDAC1 and
limits VDAC1–IP3R coupling. By altering VDAC1 gating, 225 promotes Ca2+ flux that
strengthens PERK–STIM1 association and releases them from VDAC1, enabling enhanced
VDAC1–IP3R interaction. This explains the observed co-IP changes and the rise in PERK–
STIM1 interaction (Fig. 10e, j, k). We have revised the text and model (Fig. 11) to reflect this
mechanism and anchored our interpretation to the new Ca2+-dependence and co-IP data.
Functional model: This alteration in VDAC] protein interactions yields two modules: VDAC]–
IP3R (facilitating mitochondrial Ca2+ transfer) and PERK–STIM] (ERAD inhibition), aligning
with our phenotypic readouts.
2. Compound 225 appears to have dual effects: it activates PERK, resulting in STIM1
phosphorylation, HERP1 degradation, and ERAD inhibition; while also binding to
VDAC1. However, UV-crosslinking identified VDACs as the only direct targets. How
do the authors reconcile this dual activity? Is there evidence that the STIM1–PERK
interaction is influenced by the VDAC–IP3R complex? Could the authors attempt IP
experiments to pull down VDAC using STIM1 or PERK in the presence of 225 to test
for complex formation?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s question. We reconcile the apparent “dual activity”
with a single-target model: 225 directly engages VDACs, and the PERK/STIM] phenotypes arise
secondarily from VDAC-driven Ca2+ remodeling at ER–mitochondria contact sites and
subsequently disruption of calcium homeostasis. Consistent with this, photoaffinity labeling
identifies VDAC]–3 as the only direct targets (Fig. 4a-c); CETSA shows thermal stabilization of
VDACs (Fig. 5b); MST confirms binding to recombinant VDAC] (Fig. 5a); and an in vitro
reconstituted VDAC] channel assay demonstrates 225-dependent gating modulation (Fig. 5c-e).
In addition, we do not detect 225 binding to PERK or STIM] by photoaffinity labeling (Fig. 4a-
c).
To determine whether the STIM]–PERK interaction is influenced by the VDAC–IP3R complex,
we performed co-immunoprecipitations using VDAC] as bait. VDAC] co-precipitated IP3R,
STIM], and PERK (Fig. ]0j). Treatment with 225 increased VDAC]–IP3R association while
decreasing VDAC] interactions with STIM] and PERK (Fig. ]0j). Interestingly, in first
submission, we showed that 225 enhanced the STIM]–PERK interaction (Fig. ]0e). Now we
show that both the 225-induced VDAC]–IP3R association and STIM]–PERK interaction was
attenuated by intracellular Ca2+ chelation (BAPTA-AM) (Fig. 9h, ]0k), indicating Ca2+
dependence. Collectively, these data led us to propose the working model described earlier:
under resting conditions, a PERK–STIM] complex associates with VDAC] and limits VDAC]–
IP3R coupling. By altering VDAC] gating, 225 promotes Ca2+ flux that strengthens PERK–
STIM] association and releases them from VDAC], enabling enhanced VDAC]–IP3R
interaction. Functionally, blocking IP3R or knocking down MCU reduces 225-associated
cytotoxicity, consistent with a role for the VDAC–IP3R–MCU axis in propagating mitochondrial
Ca2+ uptake and downstream effects.
3. The manuscript claims that molecule 225 selectively targets cancer cells without
affecting healthy cells. Given that VDAC1 is overexpressed in many solid tumors, did
the authors assess VDAC1 expression levels in 225-sensitive versus -insensitive cell
lines? Quantifying VDAC1 levels by RNA-seq and Western blot would help clarify
whether sensitivity to 225 correlates with VDAC1 expression and might explain the
lack of toxicity in healthy cells.
Response: We agree this is an important question with clear translational relevance. As
suggested by the reviewer, we examined VDAC1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels
in 225-sensitive versus -insensitive cell lines. We found that VDAC1 protein levels are generally
higher in sensitive cells and lower in insensitive and normal cells (Fig. 8d,e), although one
insensitive line (MDA-MB-231) exhibited unexpectedly high VDAC1 protein levels. We observed
no correlation between VDAC1 transcript abundance (analyzed public RNA-seq datasets
(https://www.proteinatlas.org) and protein levels (Fig. 8d,e vs. Fig. S8a), indicating that steady-
state VDAC1 protein abundance is likely regulated by translational efficiency or protein
stability rather than mRNA expression. Consistent with this, treatment of HeLa cells (a sensitive
line) with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib stabilized VDAC1 protein (Fig. S8b), suggesting
that VDAC1 is an unstable protein subject to proteasomal degradation. Taken together, these
findings indicate that VDAC1 protein abundance, rather than mRNA expression alone,
contributes to the differential sensitivity to 225.
4. The authors propose that molecule 225 enhances VDAC1–IP3R interaction,
promoting calcium transfer between the ER and mitochondria, which subsequently
activates PERK and drives ERAD inhibition. However, this does not fully explain the
observed increase in cytosolic calcium (Fig. 7c). Could the authors comment on the
source of the cytosolic calcium and clarify whether this increase is a direct or indirect
consequence of 225 treatment?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s question. We added new experiment using in vitro
reconstituted VDAC1 gating assay and found that 225 shifts VDAC1 into a “closed” state
favoring mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5), which is consistent with our observations that
225 increases VDAC1-IP3R interaction and calcium influx to mitochondria. We propose that
the mitochondrial calcium influx transiently lowers ER Ca2+, triggering compensatory Ca2+
influx from the extracellular space into the cytosol. The resulting elevation of cytosolic calcium
replenishes ER stores and ultimately increases calcium across the ER, cytosol, and
mitochondria, resulting in compartment-wide Ca2+ elevation, as shown in our first
submission. This model of action for 225 are supported by new data
5. The small molecule efsevin has been shown to stabilize the calcium-conductive
form of VDAC1 (PMID: 32059260). It would be informative to compare the effects of
efsevin and compound 225 on ERAD inhibition. Do both compounds share a similar
mechanism of action? Such a comparison might strengthen the proposed model.
Response: As suggested by the reviewer, we compared efsevin with compound 225 for their
effects on dislocation inhibition and on degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1. Efsevin
showed no detectable effect on dislocation or on degradation of these ERAD complex proteins
(Fig. S2a,b), indicating that its mechanism of action differs from that of compound 225.
Minor Points:
Scheme on Figure 8j should be revised to clearly depict relevant subcellular
compartments, improve image quality, and remove the pink background. Additionally,
the graph located at the bottom left appears to be an error and should be removed.
Response: The scheme has been revised as requested to clearly depict the relevant subcellular
compartments, improve image quality, and remove the pink background. The erroneous graph
at the bottom left has also been removed. The updated version now appears as Figure 11.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Key Results
This manuscript identifies a novel small molecule, NCATS-225 (“225”), as a selective
ERAD inhibitor that binds to voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs). Through a
combination of high-content screening, biochemical validation, and mechanistic
dissection, the authors suggest that 225 triggers an intracellular calcium imbalance via
a VDAC-IP3R-PERK-STIM1 signaling axis. This leads to the degradation of ERAD
complex components (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1) and induces cell death selectively in
cancer cells while sparing normal cells. The work uncovers a previously unrecognized
role for VDACs in ERAD regulation and presents a compelling chemical probe for
further study of ER proteostasis and cancer-selective cytotoxicity.
Validity
The data are of high quality, robust, and generally well-controlled. The experimental
workflow is thorough, including orthogonal validation of dislocation inhibition (GFP
reporters, CHX chase, ubiquitination assays), target identification (photoaffinity labeling
and MS), and functional studies using gene knockouts and chemical inhibitors.
However, the precise mechanism of 225 binding to VDACs and how this affects VDAC
function at a structural level remains speculative. The authors acknowledge this and
propose it as future work.
Response: Thank you for the positive assessment. In this revision, we add new evidence of direct
225–VDAC engagement by CETSA and MST (Fig. 5), complementing the photoaffinity
labeling/MS from the initial submission (Fig. 4). We also show in a reconstituted VDAC1 assay
that 225 shifts channel gating toward a lower-conductance (“closed”) state that favors
mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5). We acknowledge that the atomic binding mode and
structural basis of this effect remain to be defined and outline these as future work.
Significance
The identification of a VDAC-targeting small molecule that selectively disrupts ERAD
and kills cancer cells is novel and potentially impactful. This work opens new avenues
in cancer biology, proteostasis, and chemical biology. It also proposes an alternative
strategy to targeting UPR sensors directly — by modulating ERAD upstream. The
selective toxicity of 225 to certain cancer cell lines suggests translational relevance.
While the mechanistic basis of this selectivity is not fully resolved, the dataset
lays a solid foundation for follow-up studies.
Response: Thank you for the thoughtful comments. We agree the work is novel and impactful. In
this revision, we began to address the basis of selectivity by quantifying VDAC1 at both mRNA
and protein levels in 225-sensitive versus -insensitive lines. Protein abundance was generally
higher in sensitive lines and lower in insensitive or normal cells (Fig. 8d,e), with one outlier
(MDA-MB-231) showing high VDAC1 despite relative insensitivity. By contrast, VDAC1
transcripts from public RNA-seq (Human Protein Atlas) did not correlate with protein levels or
sensitivity (Fig. S8a). In HeLa cells, the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib stabilized VDAC1
protein (Fig. S8b), consistent with proteasomal turnover. Together, these data suggest that
VDAC1 protein abundance contributes to 225 selectivity, but additional factors must be
involved and warrants future investigations.
Data and Methodology
The methodology is state-of-the-art and spans a wide range of experimental techniques,
including high-content screening, SAR chemistry, CRISPR knockouts, calcium imaging,
and GSEA transcriptomic profiling. The description of materials and methods is detailed
and transparent. Use of the drGFP reporter for dislocation, combined with dose-
responses, time courses, and structure–activity relationships, makes the data solid.
Photoaffinity labeling with mass spectrometry is well executed, and VDAC target
identification is convincing. If available, raw calcium traces or proteomics data could be
made public in supplementary datasets.
Response: All source data for figures have been submitted in this resubmission. No
additional datasets need to be made available in public database.
Analytical Approach
Quantitative results are consistently supported by replicates, appropriate statistical
tests, and careful normalization. The use of dose-response curves, IC50 values, and
multiple replicates is appropriate. GSEA is correctly applied and complements the
mechanistic data. The authors have been transparent about sample sizes and
statistical significance thresholds.
Suggested Improvements
The authors present a compelling study identifying VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as
direct binding partners of compound 225. They propose that 225 perturbs calcium
homeostasis at the ER-mitochondria interface via these outer mitochondrial membrane
proteins, thereby inhibiting ER-associated degradation (ERAD), activating the unfolded
protein response (UPR), and triggering apoptosis. While the data are generally sound
and well-presented, I believe an alternative, structurally grounded interpretation offers a
more parsimonious explanation of the experimental findings.
Recent structural studies (Li et al., Aging 2023, DOI:10.18632/aging.205660) demonstrate that VDAC1 directly binds the ER
membrane protein complex (EMC) at ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs), locking the EMC in a non-insertase
conformation.
Earlier proteomic mapping
(Christianson, J., Olzmann, J., Shaler, T. et al. Defining human ERAD networks through an integrative mapping strategy. Nat
Cell Biol 14, 93–105 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1038/ncb2383)
showed that multiple EMC subunits interact with Derlin-1 and Derlin-2, core components of the ERAD dislocation
machinery. This raises the possibility that compound 225 inhibits ERAD not by modulating VDAC channel activity directly,
but by stabilizing a non-functional EMC–VDAC complex that disrupts EMC-dependent membrane insertion of ERAD
components such as Derlin-1.
Below, I analyze the major data types presented by the authors in support of their model and offer the alternative EMC-mediated interpretation.
1. Identification of VDAC1/2/3 as targets of 225:
The authors used a clickable photoaffinity analog of 225 to identify VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as binding targets. This result is compatible with both their interpretation (VDAC as a functional target for calcium flux regulation) and my alternative model (VDACs as structural partners of EMC, mediating 225 activity via this complex).
2. Inhibition of ERAD and activation of UPR by 225:
225 blocks degradation of NHK and HA-DeltaF508CFTR, canonical ERAD substrates. It also induces expression of BiP, CHOP, and ATF4. The authors ascribe this to ER calcium dysregulation. However, a simpler model is that 225-bound VDAC stabilizes EMC in a non-insertase state, blocking the membrane integration of Derlin-1 and other EMC-dependent ERAD components, thereby directly impairing ERAD and triggering proteostatic stress. This hypothesis explains all observed consequences (ERAD block, UPR, cell death) without invoking a poorly defined Ca2+ channeling role for VDACs.
3. Triple VDAC1 KD / VDAC2-/- / VDAC3-/- cells resist 225 phenotypes:
The authors interpret this as evidence that VDACs are the functional conduits for calcium flux perturbed by 225. However, in the alternative model, the absence of VDACs prevents 225 from stabilizing the EMC–VDAC complex. This restores EMC function and Derlin-1 insertion, preserving ERAD and preventing downstream UPR and Ca2+ dysregulation. Thus, the triple KO phenotype is compatible with both models.
Responses to comment #1-3: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments. To test possible
EMC involvement in 225’s action, we performed a series of experiments. However, our
data do not support an EMC-mediated mechanism: (1) ERAD complex degradation persists with
EMC knockdown, 225 still caused degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in EMC3, EMC4,
and EMC7 knockdown cells, similar to controls (Fig. S4e); (2) the mitochondrial Ca2+ rise
induced by 225 is unchanged by EMC3/EMC4/EMC7 knockdown (Fig. S4h); (3) the dislocation
reporter is unaffected by EMC knockdown, EMC3 or EMC7 knockdown did not alter 225’s
inhibition in the drGFP assay (Fig. S4f); and (4) VDAC–EMC interactions are unchanged by
225, VDAC1 co-IP with EMC3 or EMC4 did not increase (Fig. S4g). Together, these results do
not support EMC as the mediator of 225 activity and instead align with direct VDAC targeting
and Ca2+-dependent remodeling at ER–mitochondria contact sites.
4. ER calcium flux and 225-induced cell death:
Calcium flux is clearly altered by 225, but the authors do not provide direct
electrophysiological or structural evidence that 225 opens or blocks VDAC pores. Given
that VDAC is primarily known as a metabolite channel in the outer mitochondrial
membrane, and that Ca2+ flow between ER and mitochondria typically involves IP3R-
GRP75-VDAC tethers, it remains uncertain whether VDAC alone mediates Ca2+ leak. In
contrast, the EMC-centered model predicts that ER stress and UPR activation are
primary, and that calcium dysregulation is a downstream effect of ER proteostasis
failure.
Response: We agree that direct functional evidence is essential. As noted above, EMC is not
involved in 225’s action. We provide orthogonal target engagement (photoaffinity labeling/MS,
CETSA, MST) showing that 225 binds VDAC1 (Figs. 4-5), and we add new data using a
reconstituted VDAC1 gating assay, demonstrating that 225 shifts the channel toward a lower-
conductance (“closed”) state that favors mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Fig. 5d-e). Consistent with
ER–mitochondria tethers, 225 enhances VDAC1–IP3R association, and this remodeling is lost
with Ca2+ chelation (Figs. 9g–h, 10k). Taken together, these data support a VDAC-centered,
Ca2+-dependent mechanism for the observed flux changes and cell death, while single-channel
electrophysiology and structural mapping of the binding site remain future work.
Conclusion:
In light of published structural and proteomic data, the model in which compound 225
exerts its effects by stabilizing a non-insertase EMC–VDAC complex provides a
mechanistically unified explanation of all observed phenotypes: ERAD inhibition, UPR
activation, and calcium flux. It avoids invoking a direct gating effect of 225 on VDACs,
for which no structural or biophysical support is currently provided. I suggest the
authors consider this alternative mechanism in the discussion and test whether EMC
activity or Derlin-1 insertion is altered upon 225 treatment.
Response: Please refer Response to # 1-3 above.
This model is not incompatible with the authors' data, but may better contextualize the
role of VDACs as structural, rather than purely channel, components at MAMs. It also
makes distinct predictions about EMC dependency that could be experimentally tested.
Suggested experiments:
Assess Derlin-1 levels and membrane insertion after 225 treatment
Response: As noted above, EMC does not appear to mediate 225’s effects. Derlin-1 protein
levels were also not affected by 225 treatment (Fig. 3a); therefore, we did not assess Derlin-1
membrane insertion.
Test EMC–VDAC complex stability or conformation changes in the presence of 225
Response: We tested whether 225 alters EMC–VDAC complex stability or conformation. VDAC1
co-immunoprecipitation with EMC3 or EMC4 was unchanged in the presence of 225, indicating
no detectable effect on EMC–VDAC complex stability (Fig. S4g).
Compare 225 sensitivity in cells with EMC subunit knockdown or mutation
Response: We tested EMC involvement directly. Knockdown of EMC3, EMC4, or EMC7 did not
change (i) 225-induced degradation of ERAD complex proteins (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1), (ii) the
mitochondrial Ca2+ rise, or (iii) dislocation inhibition in the drGFP assay, and 225 did not
increase VDAC1 co-IP with EMC3/4 (Fig. S4). Because these activity-linked readouts were
unchanged, EMC loss did not appear to modulate 225 sensitivity; therefore, we did not pursue
additional viability assays in EMC-mutant backgrounds.
Clarity and Context
The manuscript is clearly written and accessible. Figures are well designed and support
the main conclusions. The discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within
existing literature and discusses limitations transparently. The novelty of VDACs in
ERAD is well supported.
References
The referencing is thorough and appropriate. Key prior work on ERAD, UPR, VDAC
function, and chemical screening is cited. I did not note any major omissions.
Your Expertise
My expertise includes ER proteostasis and chemical biology. I am confident in
assessing the main findings and mechanistic claims. I did not independently evaluate
the full MS data or chemical synthesis protocols but found the presented validation
to be sufficient.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed
reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in
peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers
who co-review manuscripts.
Response: Thank you for co-reviewing our manuscript as part of Nature Communications ’
initiative to train and recognize Early Career Researchers. We appreciate the time and
thoughtful evaluation from both you and your co-reviewer.
Point-to-point response to the Reviewers
We are grateful for the opportunity to resubmit our revised manuscript and sincerely thank
Reviewers #1, #2, #4, and #5 for their positive recommendations for acceptance in Nature
Communications. We also appreciate the constructive comments from Reviewer #3 and have
revised the data accordingly. We believe that the thoughtful feedback from all reviewers has
substantially improved the quality of the manuscript.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
I would like to thank the authors for their comprehensive response to my previous
comments. The additional data and revisions have significantly improved the
manuscript, and I am impressed with the work. I am happy to recommend the
manuscript for acceptance. Congratulations to the team on a fine piece of research!
Response:
We sincerely thank Reviewer #1 for the positive evaluation and encouraging comments. We
greatly appreciate your support and are pleased that the revisions have strengthened the
manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have successfully addressed my comments. No additional questions.
Response:
We thank Reviewer #2 for acknowledging that our revisions have addressed all prior comments.
We appreciate your time and consideration in reviewing our manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have satisfactorily addressed all my previous concerns, many of which
were also raised by the other reviewers. In particular, the additional experiments now
provide stronger support for their proposed working model. The revised data establish a
clear mechanism of action for compound 225, which stabilizes the VDAC1–IP3R
interaction at the expense of STIM1 and PERK association.
I appreciate the authors’ efforts to confirm the direct binding of 225 to VDAC1 using
orthogonal approaches, including electrophysiological assays that demonstrate an
effect on VDAC1 gating consistent with stabilization of its closed state. However, I have
one remaining point of clarification. The reported dissociation constant (Kd) of ~3 μM for
225–VDAC1 interaction (as determined by MST) suggests a moderate affinity. Given
this, why were the bilayer experiments performed using only 400 nM compound? At
such a concentration—well below the K_D—binding would be expected to be minimal.
Indeed, the dose–response curve in Figure 5a suggests little to no effect at this
concentration, yet the electrophysiological recordings show a measurable change in
G/G_max. While binding and functional efficacy are not necessarily identical processes,
binding must occur for an effect to be observed. How do the authors reconcile this
apparent discrepancy between binding affinity and electrophysiological response at sub-
Kd concentrations (200–400 nM)?
Along similar lines, in Figure 5c, the representative traces appear to have been acquired
at different voltages across the conditions (±60 mV for control, ±40 mV for 200 nM 225,
and ±30 mV for 400 nM 225). Could the authors clarify the rationale behind using
different potentials for each condition? For better comparison, I suggest presenting
representative traces recorded at the same voltages for all experimental conditions, or
alternatively including a supplemental figure showing the full voltage range. As currently
presented, it is difficult to directly appreciate the effect of compound 225 across
conditions in Figure 5c.
Response:
Our orthogonal validation demonstrates that compound 225 exhibits a highly favorable, context-
dependent mechanism of target engagement. We confirmed direct target engagement with a 3
µM binding affinity using Microscale Thermophoresis (MST). However, when we assessed the
compound in a physiologically relevant functional assay, using VDAC1 reconstituted into its
native membrane environment, we observed a significantly enhanced functional potency of 400
nM. This 7.5-fold increase in potency is a key finding. It indicates that the compound's activity is
optimized in the correct biological context. The most plausible explanation is a membrane-
induced conformational change: VDAC1 likely adopts its specific, functional conformation only
within a true lipid bilayer. 225 appears to have a much higher affinity for this active, membrane-
embedded state. The MST assay, which measures an average affinity across all conformations in
detergent, reports a weaker value. This model is strongly supported by our cellular data, which
shows an IC50 of 1 µM in inhibiting dislocation in cells, a context where VDAC1 is naturally
anchored in the lipid membrane. Therefore, we have high confidence that the sub-micromolar
potencies (400 nM - 1 µM) are the biologically and therapeutically relevant metrics,
demonstrating that our compound is a potent and functionally active inhibitor of VDAC1.
Following the Reviewer's helpful suggestion, we modified Figure 5c and present the single-
channel current traces at the same applied voltages from -30 to 60 mV for each condition. The
lowest voltages at which VDAC1 gating was observed in control and in the presence of 225 are
indicated by arrows.The corresponding discussion has been added to the revised manuscript
(page 12 in red).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
I am happy with (and impressed by!) the new data gathered and presented and I
recommend the manuscript for publication.
Response:
We thank Reviewer #4 for the positive and encouraging comments. We greatly appreciate your
recognition of the new data and are pleased that our revisions meet your expectations.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports.
This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review
and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review
manuscripts.
Response:
We thank Reviewer #5 for the co-review and appreciate Nature Communications’ initiative to
support and recognize Early Career Researchers in the peer review process.
REVIEWERS' COMMENTS
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I thank the authors for their thorough and thoughtful response to my previous
comments. The additional data and revisions have substantially strengthened the
manuscript, and I am pleased with the improvements made. However, I noticed that the
scale bars in Fig. 5c are now missing, whereas they were present in the previous
version of the manuscript. Aside from this minor issue, I am happy to recommend the
manuscript for acceptance.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful and positive evaluation of our work, as well
as for the helpful comments that have strengthened the manuscript. We apologize for the
oversight regarding Fig. 5c, and the missing scale bar has now been added in the revised version.

## Paper

## Abstract

Endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) is a critical protein quality control mechanism that also regulates lipid metabolism and calcium homeostasis. Dysregulation of ERAD and unfolded protein response underlies diseases including cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic syndromes. Small molecule modulators of ERAD could enable mechanistic discovery and therapeutic intervention, but few have been identified. Using a high-content screening, we discovered several ERAD-modulating compounds, including NCATS-SM0225, an ERAD inhibitor that unexpectedly binds all three isoforms of VDAC, outer mitochondrial membrane proteins enriched at mitochondria-associated membranes. This led us to discover an essential role for VDACs in ERAD and ER-phagy. NCATS-SM0225 elevates cytosolic, ER, and mitochondrial calcium through calcium influx and IP3R–MCU activity. This calcium imbalance strengthens VDAC1–IP3R coupling and activates PERK, which phosphorylates STIM1 and drives degradation of key ERAD regulators. Loss of these components amplifies PERK signaling and selectively kills cancer cells while sparing normal cells. These findings uncover a cancer-specific role of VDACs in ERAD regulation and calcium signaling, highlighting a therapeutically actionable vulnerability.

---

## Introduction

The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a central organelle responsible for protein folding, lipids synthesis, and calcium homeostasis, essential for maintaining cellular proteostasis. ER-associated degradation (ERAD) is a critical quality control mechanism in which misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are recognized, retrotranslocated to the cytosolic surface for ubiquitination and dislocation, and subsequently delivered to the proteasome for degradation1–6. Beyond protein quality control, ERAD also regulates physiological processes such as lipid metabolism and calcium signaling by selectively degrading transcription factors, enzymes, and regulatory proteins often in a cell type-specific manner3,7,8. ERAD is closely coordinated with ER-phagy, a selective autophagy process that degrades ER fragments and misfolded proteins, compensating for ERAD deficiencies and protecting the ER from dysfunction3,9,10. Insufficient removal and subsequent accumulation of misfolded proteins lead to ER stress and activates the unfolded protein response (UPR)11,12. The UPR is mediated by three ER stress sensors—IRE1α, ATF6, and PERK—which work to restore proteostasis. However, severe or prolonged ER stress can shift the UPR toward pro-apoptotic signaling13–15. While the UPR is critical for maintaining the function of secretory cells like pancreatic β-cells and B lymphocytes, it is also implicated in diseases such as cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic syndromes14,16–19.

In neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, Huntington’s, Parkinson’s and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, toxic protein aggregates disrupt ERAD, causing chronic ER stress and neuronal cell death via pro-apoptotic UPR signaling20–28. In contrast, cancer cells often experience ER stress due to disrupted protein homeostasis; in this context, the UPR is reprogrammed to promote survival, tumorigenesis, metastasis, drug resistance, and immune evasion16,18,29,30. UPR activation has been documented in many human cancers, including breast, pancreatic, lung, prostate, brain, and hematologic malignancies16,30. Small-molecule inhibitors targeting specific UPR branches have been developed to explore therapeutic potential but overlapping functions and compensatory mechanisms may limit their efficacies31,32.

Modulating ERAD activity represents a promising strategy to influence ER stress and UPR signaling, as misfolded protein accumulation is the primary driver of ER stress. Enhancing or inhibiting ERAD can either promote clearance or exacerbate accumulation of misfolded proteins, respectively, thereby shaping cellular stress responses31,33,34. The development of potent and selective small molecule ERAD modulators as chemical biology tools is an important step towards dissecting ERAD mechanisms and roles in physiology and disease. ERAD modulators also offer therapeutic potential by enhancing ERAD to alleviate ER stress in neurodegenerative diseases and diabetes or suppressing ERAD to sensitize cancer cells to stress-induced apoptosis33–35. However, only a limited number of ERAD modulators have been identified to date, and the field remains underdeveloped.

In this study, we present the development of a high-content phenotypic screening assay designed to identify small molecule modulators of ERAD. Among the compounds screened, NCATS-SM0225 (referred to as 225) emerged as a potent ERAD inhibitor, but unexpectedly, it was found to bind to voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs). Binding of 225 to VDACs triggers IP3R-MCU-dependent disruption of calcium homeostasis, which subsequently activates a calcium-PERK-STIM1 signaling. This cascade leads to the degradation of key ERAD complex proteins (HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1) and selectively induces cancer cell death while sparing normal cells. These findings provide critical insights into ERAD biology, its interplay with calcium signaling, and its potential as a cancer therapeutic target. This work highlights the utility of small molecule modulators in probing ERAD function and towards developing first-in-class cancer-selective therapies.
