## Results

High-content screening for small molecule modulators of ERAD
During ERAD, misfolded proteins are recognized and retained in the ER, where luminal chaperones and lectins facilitate their delivery to ERAD complexes for retrotranslocation to the cytosol1,6. This process is essential for ERAD, as it enables misfolded proteins to be ubiquitinated and subsequently degraded by the proteasome. We have previously developed the drGFP reporter assay to monitor the final step of retrotranslocation, the complete dislocation of substrate proteins from the ER into the cytosol, in live cells36. This assay utilizes split GFP37, which reconstitutes fluorescence upon successful dislocation in the presence of a proteasome inhibitor, which provides a direct, real-time readout of ERAD activity (Fig. 1a, and Supplementary Movies 1–3). The null Hong Kong variant of α−1-antitrypsin (NHK), an ER luminal misfolded protein, was selected as the ERAD substrate (NHK-drGFP) in the primary screen, where changes in GFP intensity were visualized and quantified to assess ERAD activity36. CD3δ, an ER membrane substrate, was used in the drGFP (CD3δ-drGFP) assay as a secondary screen to confirm primary hits. Enhanced substrate dislocation increases GFP fluorescence, while inhibition (e.g., NMS-873-ap97/VCP inhibitor, in Fig. 1a) suppresses it, making this a powerful tool for studying ERAD and identifying potential modulators.

We first miniaturized and optimized the drGFP assay in 1536-well format to enable high-throughput screening. Pilot screening indicated robust assay performance (Supplementary Fig. 1a) with reproducible dose-dependent inhibition observed for p97/VCP inhibitor NMS-873, known to inhibit dislocation (Fig. 1b). The optimized assay was used to perform a screen of 96,047 compounds, which exhibited a favorable signal window (Fig. 1c) and a robust mean Z’ factor of 0.59 (Supplementary Fig. 1b). The primary screen yielded 956 hits, comprised of approved drugs, bioactive tool compounds, and diversity-collection molecules (Fig. 1d, and Supplementary Fig. 1c). We focused on the 419 compounds that originated from the diversity collections and retested them at 11 concentrations spanning 37 nM to 38 μM. Sixty-six compounds were confirmed as inhibitors, using the criteria of AC50 < 20 μM and > 60% efficacy. The hits were then tested in a second model of ER dislocation, using a misfolded CD3δ-based drGFP, with 62 of the 66 compounds (94%) categorized as active using the same 20 μM and 60% inhibition criteria. The 62 compounds represented thirteen chemotypes. Following removal of acutely cytotoxic compounds (showing cytotoxicity after 4 h treatment) and compounds with covalent warheads, six compounds, representing six chemotypes, were prioritized for further analysis (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Figs. 1d, e).

We next tested the six potential dislocation inhibitors for their effects on the stability of ΔF508CFTR, a well-established ERAD substrate and the cystic fibrosis-causing protein38,39. Baby hamster kidney fibroblasts (BHK) stably expressing HA-ΔF508CFTR (HA-ΔF508CFTR-BHK cells)40,41 were treated with the putative inhibitors for 24 h. The results revealed that only 225 significantly increased the levels of HA-ΔF508CFTR in both the ER (core-glycosylated B form) and at the cell surface (fully glycosylated mature C form) (Fig. 1f). These increases are likely due to the inhibition of HA-ΔF508CFTR degradation, which promotes its forward trafficking (Fig. 1f). Notably, the non-glycosylated form of ΔF508CFTR (A form) was not observed in either control or 225-treated cells (Fig. 1f), suggesting that 225 affects the degradation and trafficking of the glycosylated forms of ΔF508CFTR40,41. Next, we resynthesized 225 (methods section) and tested the multiple batches in parallel. All the batches consistently showed reproducible activity in the dislocation assay (Supplementary Fig. 1f). To further validate and potentially improve the activity of 225, we designed and conducted a focused structure–activity relationship (SAR) study by synthesizing several structural analogs (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Note 1). Smaller substituents on the phenyl ring were generally tolerated and, in some cases, slightly improved potency (Supplementary Fig. 2; compounds 1-5). However, all other structural changes investigated (a subset which is included here) resulted in a significant loss of activity, including: the addition of alkyl groups in the benzylic position, N-alkylation of the sulfonamide, lactone-opening to various amides, truncation of the benzyl-sulfonamide altogether to parent amine, and changing sulfonamide to the analogous amide (Supplementary Fig. 2; compounds 6-10, respectively).

Validation of 225 as a dislocation inhibitor
Time-lapse imaging of the NHK-drGFP reporter showed that 225 inhibited dislocation as demonstrated by a dose-dependent reduction in drGFP, with an IC50 of 1.02 μM (Fig. 2a–c, and Supplementary Movies 4–7). Since inhibition of dislocation is expected to block ERAD, we further evaluated the effects of 225 on the degradation of NHK and an ER membrane substrate CD3δ, using cycloheximide (CHX) chase. Consistent with its role as a dislocation inhibitor, 225 significantly inhibited the degradation of both substrates (Fig. 2d–g). For ER luminal substrates, dislocation is a prerequisite for ubiquitination, as ubiquitination occurs on the cytosolic surface of the ER. As expected, 225 effectively inhibited NHK ubiquitination (Fig. 2h). These findings collectively establish 225 as a potent inhibitor of ERAD dislocation.

225 induces selective degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in HeLa cells
Inhibition of ERAD is expected to induce ER stress and activate the unfolded protein response (UPR). To explore the effects of 225 on UPR signaling and ERAD-related proteins in HeLa cells, we performed immunoblotting (IB) analyses, using tunicamycin (Tm) as a positive control for ER stress. Remarkably, treatment with 225 for 24-h resulted in a significant downregulation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1, accompanied by a phosphorylation-induced mobility shift of PERK (Fig. 3a), with the effects being both dose- and time-dependent. In addition, there was a modest downregulation of Sel1L protein (Fig. 3a). To determine whether the reduction in HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 levels was due to post-translational degradation, HeLa cells were treated with 225 alone or in combination with either the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib (BTZ) or the lysosome inhibitor chloroquine (CQ). All three proteins were stabilized by BTZ but not CQ (Supplementary Fig. 3a), indicating that 225 promotes their proteasomal degradation. Consistently, 225 did not decrease HERP1, OS9, or SEL1L mRNA; only FAM8A1 showed a modest reduction (Supplementary Fig. 3b).

Given that p97/VCP facilitates the extraction of ubiquitinated misfolded proteins from the ER for proteasomal degradation42, we investigated whether 225 targets HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 through the ERAD pathway. Treatment with p97/VCP inhibitors DBeQ and NMS-87343,44 effectively blocked the 225-induced degradation of all three proteins (Supplementary Fig. 3c), confirming their degradation via the ERAD-proteasome pathway. Consistent with these findings, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of transcriptome data from 225-treated HeLa cells revealed significant enrichment of UPR activation (Fig. 3b), which was further validated by IB (Fig. 3c). Notably, PERK signaling emerged as the most prominently activated pathway (Fig. 3b, d). Inhibition of PERK kinase activity partially rescued HeLa cell death induced by 225 (Fig. 3e). Together, these results demonstrate that 225 disrupts protein dislocation, induces the degradation of ERAD complex proteins, and activates PERK-mediated proapoptotic signaling.

225 selectively targets all three isoforms of VDAC (voltage-dependent anion channel)
To identify the molecular target of 225, a diazirine-based photoaffinity and clickable probe (225-cc, Supplementary Fig. 4c) was synthesized by incorporating 225 with a minimally interfering photo-affinity label (MI-PAL)45 to enable target identification studies (Fig. 4a, b). First, we confirmed that 225-cc retained dislocation inhibitory activity, with an IC50 of 9.8 μM in the NHK-drGFP assay (Supplementary Figs. 4a, b). Next, cells treated with 225-cc were irradiated with UV light (365 nm) to induce diazirine photolytic conversion into a reactive carbene, capable of covalent insertion into amino acid residues in close proximity. To identify 225-cc target proteins, a commercially available trifunctional probe, DdeTAMRA Biotin Azide, which contains a fluorescent dye and a chemically cleavable biotin pull-down handle (Supplementary Fig. 4c), was used to label 225-cc-bound proteins via copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC; ‘click’ reaction)46 (Supplementary Fig. 4d). The 225-cc-labeled proteins, now covalently bound to a fluorescent moiety, could be visualized on SDS-PAGE gels (Fig. 4a), and the biotin tag facilitated identification by mass spectrometry (MS) following affinity capture using streptavidin beads (Fig. 4b). These experiments indicated that 225-cc is quite selective, as a single protein band of approximately 35 kDa was observed in both total cell lysates and streptavidin pull down samples (Fig. 4a). MS analysis of the protein band pulled down by streptavidin beads revealed that the top three identified proteins were the three isoforms of VDAC, outer mitochondrial membrane proteins also localized in mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs)47,48 (Fig. 4b). Knockout of each VDAC isoform reduced 225 labeling to an extent consistent with the reported expression levels in HeLa cells49, with VDAC1 showing the most significant reduction (Fig. 4c). These results indicate that 225 binds to all three isoforms of VDAC.

The ER membrane protein complex (EMC) is an ER insertase, and recent reports suggest VDAC1 can associate with EMC via EMC3, EMC4, and EMC750. To further probe target specificity, we tested whether EMC mediates 225’s effects. Degradation of ERAD components (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1) persisted in 225-treated EMC3-, EMC4-, and EMC7-knockdown cells, similar to controls, and 225 did not affect the levels of these three EMC proteins (Supplementary Fig. 4e); EMC3 or EMC7 knockdown also did not alter 225-mediated dislocation inhibition in the drGFP assay (Supplementary Fig. 4f); and VDAC–EMC interactions were unchanged by 225 as demonstrated by VDAC1 co-IP with EMC3 or EMC4 (Supplementary Fig. 4g). These results do not support an EMC-dependent mechanism of 225 and further substantiate VDACs as the specific targets of 225.

As VDACs are not known to control ERAD but have been recently isolated as interacting proteins for SEL1L, a key cofactor for the HRD1 ERAD E3 ubiquitin ligase51, we next investigated the potential connection by knocking down each of the three VDAC isoforms and assessing the effects on NHK dislocation using NHK-drGFP reporter. Surprisingly, single knockdown of any VDAC isoform by itself markedly inhibited dislocation (Fig. 4d, e), supporting a role for VDACs in ERAD. Given the marked effects on dislocation, it was surprising that we succeeded in establishing viable VDAC KO cell lines (Fig. 4c), suggesting that a compensatory mechanism was activated to protect cells from the effects of dislocation inhibition. Since ER-phagy is a key compensatory response to ERAD inhibition9,52,53, we monitored ER-phagy activity using the well-established ss-RFP-GFP-KDEL reporter54 stably expressed in HeLa cells. Knockdown of each VDAC isoform activated ER-phagy, as indicated by a decrease in the GFP/RFP ratio (Fig. 4f) and the formation of RFP puncta accompanied (Fig. 4g). Similarly, knockdown of VDAC1 led to the relocalization of CD3δ-mCherry into puncta and a decrease in its cellular levels (Fig. 4h, i). These findings demonstrate that 225 selectively targets all three isoforms of VDAC and suggest that VDACs play a critical role in maintaining ERAD activity. The activation of ER-phagy following VDAC knockdown suggests that ER-phagy sequesters and degrades ERAD substrates, thereby reducing their dislocation from the ER.

225 directly interacts with VDAC1 and regulates its function in vitro
To validate the binding of 225 to the identified target proteins, we conducted microscale thermophoresis (MST) analysis. The equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) between 225 and recombinant human VDAC1 was determined to be 3.13 μM, indicating direct binding (Fig. 5a). To further examine 225 binding to VDACs in cells, we employed the Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA), which is based on the principle that ligand binding increases the thermal stability of its target protein, allowing detection of the stabilized protein in the soluble cellular fraction by immunoblotting or mass spectrometry55,56. Treatment with 225 increased the thermal stability of all three VDAC isoforms but not the control protein ATP5A (Fig. 5b). Together, these results provide strong evidence for a direct interaction between 225 and VDACs.

To examine if 225 binding to VDAC1 affects its channel function, we employed a voltage-clamp electrophysiology approach on a system of the recombinant human VDAC1 reconstituted into a planar lipid membrane57,58. This method allowed us to perform highly sensitive measurements of functional interaction between 225 and VDAC1 at the single-molecule level and to investigate the impact of 225 on VDAC1 basic properties, such as its single-channel conductance and voltage gating. The planar lipid membranes were formed from a mixture of dioleoyl-phosphatidylcholine (DOPC):dioleoyl-phosphatidylethanolamine (DOPE) (1:1 w/w), two major phospholipids of the mitochondrial outer membrane59,60, in symmetrical 1 M KCl buffer solution. Under these conditions, VDAC1 typically forms ion channels of ~4.0 nS conductance, which characteristically gate, i.e., transition from the high conducting “open” state to a variety of low conducting or “closed” states in response to the applied voltages61,62. In control, 225-free, experiments, the application of +/− 60 mV was required to observe consistent voltage gating (Fig. 5c). The addition of 225 at 200 nM and 400 nM concentrations resulted in VDAC1 gating at much lower amplitudes of negative potentials, specifically at −40 mV and −30 mV (indicated by arrows in Fig. 5c). This resulted in a 20–30 mV shift of the voltage required for gating of a single VDAC1 channel, compared to the control conditions (Fig. 5c). Thus, 225 promotes VDAC1 closure at reduced voltages in a concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 5c).

Quantification of voltage-gating and obtaining a 225 binding curve requires a statistical analysis of the gating of many channels. The multichannel experiments were performed under the application of slow triangular voltage waves (5 mHz, +/− 60 mV), which enable a slow channel closure and fast reopening, and allow us to collect responses of 50-100 channels to the applied voltages63,64. Figure 5d shows the normalized conductance-voltage plots at negative potentials (G/Gmax vs voltage), where G is the conductance at a given voltage and Gmax is the maximum conductance at voltages close to 0 mV. The multichannel measurements were performed under the same experimental conditions as single-channel measurements (Fig. 5c). The addition of 225 to the cis side of the membrane, enhanced VDAC1 gating by decreasing the minimum conductance (Gmin), calculated at |V| > 50 mV, in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 5d). Notably, the increased voltage-gating was observed in single- and multichannel experiments predominantly at potentials that are negative from the side of 225 addition, the cis side of the membrane. The gating response to 225 addition was quantified as normalized change in conductance, (Gmax - Gmin)/Gmin, and plotted versus 225 concentrations (Fig. 5e). These results point to a direct functional interaction between 225 and VDAC1. We can speculate that by promoting the VDAC1 closed state, 225 promotes calcium influx to mitochondria47,65, thus regulating calcium signaling through direct interaction with VDAC1.

225 induces calcium elevation in mitochondria, ER, and cytosol, leading to HERP1 and OS9 degradation
VDAC, the most abundant protein in the mitochondrial outer membrane, plays a critical role in regulating calcium influx, metabolism, and cell death47,66–69. To investigate the effects of 225 on intracellular calcium dynamics, we monitored calcium levels in mitochondria, cytosol, and ER using established fluorescent calcium sensors, including the cytosol calcium sensor GCaMP6F, the mitochondrial calcium sensor Mitycam, and the ER calcium sensor GCaMPer70. We observed that 225 induced a dose- and time-dependent increase in calcium levels across all three compartments (Fig. 6a–c). KO of individual VDAC isoforms or dual VDAC2/3 reduced 225-induced calcium elevation, while RNAi-mediated knockdown (KD) of VDAC1 in the context of VDAC2/3 KO (VDAC1KD/VDAC2-/-/VDAC3-/-) nearly abolished the effect of 225 on calcium levels across all compartments (Fig. 6d–f). Furthermore, VDACs were found to mediate 225-induced cell death, as measured by caspase-3/7 activation (Fig. 6g, h). Loss of all three VDAC isoforms significantly diminished 225-induced cell death (Fig. 6i), further supporting the conclusion that VDACs are the molecular targets through which 225 elevates intracellular calcium and triggers cell death. As a negative control, EMC knockdown did affect 225-induced increase in mitochondrial calcium (Supplementary Fig. 4h).

To determine whether calcium elevation mediates 225-induced cytotoxicity, we used the calcium chelator BAPTA-AM to sequester intracellular calcium during 225 treatment of HeLa cells. Calcium chelation completely abolished 225-induced cell death (Fig. 6j). Moreover, BAPTA-AM treatment prevented 225-induced degradation of HERP1 and OS9 (Fig. 6k). These findings suggest that 225 binds to VDACs, triggering a rise in intracellular calcium levels that subsequently induces the degradation of HERP1 and OS9 and ultimately leads to cell death.

Given reports that efsevin stabilizes the calcium-conductive state of VDAC71, we tested it alongside 225 in our ERAD assays. Under identical conditions, efsevin neither impaired dislocation nor reduced HERP1 or OS9 protein levels, whereas 225 robustly inhibited dislocation and decreased HERP1/OS9 (Supplementary Fig. 6a). These data indicate that efsevin does not inhibit ERAD in our system and support a mechanism for 225 that is distinct from efsevin.

225 preferentially targets a subgroup of cancer cells while sparing normal cells
To determine the potential cell type-dependent effects of 225, we randomly examined 16 different cancer cell lines derived from various cancers, including melanoma, glioma, breast cancer, liver cancer, pancreatic cancer, osteosarcoma, and mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Treatment with 225 induced the degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in 11 out of the 16 cancer cell lines while showing minimal or no effects in the remaining 5 cell lines (Fig. 7a). Notably, 225 had no impact on the protein levels of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1 in three types of primary normal human cells, including fibroblasts from three individuals, epidermal melanocytes, and hepatocytes (Fig. 7a). Importantly, the cytotoxicity of 225 showed a strong positive correlation with the degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1, with degradation-resistant cells showing limited cytotoxicity (Fig. 7a, b). The differential cytotoxicity of 225 was further validated by measuring caspase-3/7 activation (Supplementary Figs. 7a–d). Remarkably, the viability of normal cells was not impacted by 225 up to 10 μM concentrations that impacted cancer cells (Fig. 7b, Supplementary Fig. 7d) and concentrations up to 50 μM had no effect on primary human hepatocytes (Supplementary Fig. 7f). These results suggest that 225 selectively targets a subgroup of cancer cells while sparing normal cells, and this selectivity strongly correlates with its ability to induce the degradation of HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1.

To obtain proof-of-concept evidence for the antitumor efficacy of 225, we evaluated its activity in vivo using A375 melanoma xenografts, a 225-sensitive cancer model. Daily intraperitoneal administration of 225 (20 mg/kg) markedly inhibited tumor growth without detectable toxicity (Fig. 7c–e). Treated mice exhibited no clinical signs of adverse effects, and histological examination of the liver, pancreas, and kidney revealed no abnormalities (Supplementary Figs. 7g–i). Collectively, these results identify VDAC as a promising cancer-selective therapeutic target.

225-induced intracellular calcium elevation is a defining feature of its selective cytotoxicity
225 induces elevation of calcium in cytosol, mitochondria, and ER and causes death in HeLa cells (Fig. 6). Next, we examined whether this calcium elevation differentiates the selective cytotoxicity using 225-sensitive MCF7ca, A375, and A253 cells, and 225-insensitive MDA-MB-231, T47D, MDA-MD-453 cells, as well as primary human fibroblasts (HDFa, GM05294) as examples. Calcium increases were observed only in 225-sensitive cancer cells, with no significant changes observed in 225-insentitive cancer cells and primary human fibroblasts (Fig. 8a–c). These findings suggest that 225 preferentially targets a subgroup of cancer cells by disrupting calcium homeostasis and inducing the degradation of ERAD complex proteins, while sparing normal cells and a subgroup of cancer cells.

VDAC1 expression is frequently overexpressed in various cancers compared to normal cells and is associated with poor prognosis and tumor progression72,73. Next, we examined whether VDAC1 expression contributes to the differential sensitivity of 225. We found that VDAC1 protein levels are generally higher in sensitive cells and lower in insensitive or normal cells (Fig. 8d, e); however, one insensitive cell line (MDA-MB-231) expresses high levels of VDAC1 protein (Fig. 8d, e). Although the underlying mechanism that confer resistance of MDA-MB-231 to 225 are not understood, we speculate that mutations may alter downstream death-signaling pathways. We also analyzed mRNA expression data from the Human Protein Atlas74,75 and found no correlation between VDAC1 transcript abundance and protein levels (Fig. 8d-e vs. Supplementary Fig. 8a). This suggests that steady-state VDAC1 protein abundance is regulated by translational efficiency or protein stability rather than transcription. Consistent with this possibility, treatment of HeLa cells (a sensitive line) with the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib markedly stabilized VDAC proteins (Supplementary Fig. 8b), indicating that VDACs are an unstable protein subject to proteasomal degradation, thereby affecting their steady-state protein levels. Taken together, these new findings suggest that VDAC1 protein abundance may contribute to the differential sensitivity to 225.

Calcium influx and IP3R activity mediate 225-induced intracellular calcium elevation and cell death
The 225-induced increase in intracellular calcium is likely driven by calcium influx from the extracellular space. This was confirmed by the failure of 225 to elevate intracellular calcium when HeLa cells were cultured in calcium-free medium (Fig. 9a–c). The simultaneous increase in calcium levels across the ER, mitochondria, and cytosol suggests that 225 broadly disrupts calcium homeostasis following VDAC binding. One potential mediator of these effects is the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP3R), as IP3R, grp75, and VDAC form a complex at mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs) that facilitates calcium transport from the ER to mitochondria76. To test this hypothesis, cells were treated with the IP3R inhibitor 2-APB77. 2-APB effectively inhibited 225-induced calcium increases in all three subcellular compartments and reduced cytotoxicity (Fig. 9d, e), implicating IP3R as a mediator of changes in calcium homeostasis. Furthermore, 2-APB also blocked 225-induced PERK activation and the degradation of HERP1 and OS9 (Fig. 9f). Coimmunoprecipitation experiments revealed that 225 significantly enhances the interaction between VDAC1 and IP3R in calcium-dependent manner (Fig. 9g, h), consistent with 225 altering complexes at the MAMs that control calcium. Inhibiting the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU), which is specifically responsible for the uptake of calcium into the mitochondrial matrix78, also diminished the cytotoxicity of 225 (Fig. 9i). These findings suggest that 225 binding to VDAC1 enhances the VDAC1-IP3R interaction, facilitates a rise in calcium levels across intracellular compartments, activates PERK, and triggers degradation of ERAD complex proteins, which ultimately culminates in cell death.

STIM1 regulates 225-induced calcium influx, and its phosphorylation mediates 225-induced ERAD complex degradation and cell death
The observations that 225-induced intracellular calcium dynamic changes require (1) extracellular calcium influx (Figs. 9a–c) and (2) ER contributions, mediated by IP3R (Fig. 9d, e), led us to hypothesize that STIM1, a key regulator of store-operated calcium entry (SOCE), might contribute to these events79,80. To investigate this possibility, we knocked down STIM1 and measured its effects on intracellular calcium levels. STIM1 knockdown disrupted cellular calcium homeostasis, as reflected by increased calcium levels in the ER, cytosol, and mitochondria to varying degrees (Fig. 10a). Notably, 225 failed to further elevate calcium levels in STIM1-KD cells (Fig. 10b), suggesting that STIM1 regulates 225-induced calcium elevation.

While elevated calcium is generally toxic to cells, STIM1 knockdown unexpectedly diminished 225-induced cytotoxicity and reduced PERK expression (Fig. 10c, d). This result is consistent with experiments identifying PERK as a crucial mediator of 225-induced cell death (Fig. 3e). Coimmunoprecipitation experiments revealed that STIM1 interacts with PERK, and 225 enhanced this interaction (Fig. 10e). Given that PERK is activated by 225, we investigated whether PERK phosphorylates STIM1. Indeed, 225 induced a mobility shift in STIM1, and the Phos-Tag assay confirmed that this shift was due to phosphorylation (Fig. 10f, g). The 225-induced phosphorylation of STIM1 was inhibited by the PERK inhibitor GSK2606414 (Fig. 10f). Furthermore, PERK inhibition, like STIM1 knockdown, diminished 225-induced degradation of HERP1 and OS9 (Fig. 10f). Consistently, PERK knockdown reduced 225-induced inhibition of NHK dislocation (Fig. 10h, i). These findings indicate that 225 activates PERK, which phosphorylates STIM1, resulting in the degradation of HERP1 and OS9 and inhibition of ERAD.

STIM1 and PERK have not been previously reported to interact with VDAC1. To determine how 225 binding to VDAC1 could affect their association, we measured potential interactions among these proteins using co-immunoprecipitation (coIP). VDAC1 was found to interact with STIM1 and PERK in addition to IP3R (Fig. 10j). Interestingly, treatment with 225 enhanced the VDAC1–IP3R interaction but reduced its association with STIM1 and PERK (Fig. 10j). Concomitantly, 225 increased STIM1–PERK complex formation, which was dependent on calcium but independent of PERK kinase activity (Fig. 10k, l). These results suggest that 225 binding to VDAC1 elevates intracellular calcium levels, thereby remodeling the interaction network among VDAC1, IP3R, STIM1, and PERK. The increased VDAC1–IP3R interaction further amplifies calcium influx, while enhanced PERK–STIM1 association and PERK-mediated STIM1 phosphorylation destabilize HERP1, OS9, and FAM8A1. Collectively, these events coincide with sustained calcium elevation, culminating in cell death (see model in Figur S9).

## Methods

Cell culture
HeLa (CCL-2), HepG2 (HB-8065), A-375 (CRL-1619), U-2OS (HTB-96), A253 (HTB-41), PSN1 (CRL-3211), Primary Dermal Fibroblast (HDFa, PCS-201-012) and Primary Epidermal Melanocyte (HEMa, PCS-200-013) cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, USA). U-251MG (09063001) and U-87MG (89081402) were obtained from Millipore Sigma. Normal untransformed fibroblast GM05294 and GM04390 cell lines were purchased from Coriell Institute. MDA-MB-231 (CRM-HTB-26), MDA-MB-453 (HTB-131), SK-BR-3 (HTB-30), BT474 (HTB-20), T-47D (HTB-133), and MIAPaCa-2 (CRL-1420) cell lines were obtained from Dr. Mark J. Henderson (NCATS/NIH). MCF7ca (MCF7 human breast cancer cell lines transfected with aromatase gene) cells were obtained from Dr. Yun Qiu (University of Maryland, Baltimore). Hepatocyte and Huh7 cells were obtained from Dr. Hongbing Wang (University of Maryland, Baltimore). HeLa cells stably expressing SP-S11-NHK-HA and S1-10 were established previously36.

All cell lines were maintained at 37°C in a 5% CO₂ humidified incubator. GM05294 and GM04390 were cultured in Minimum Essential Medium (MEM). HDFa was maintained in Fibroblast Basal Medium (ATCC® PCS-201-030™) supplemented with Fibroblast Growth Kit-Serum-free (ATCC® PCS-201-040™), HEMa is maintained in Dermal Cell Basal Medium (ATCC PCS-200-030) supplemented with Adult Melanocyte Growth Kit (ATCC PCS-200-042). PSN1 and T-47D were cultured in RPMI-1640 Medium. MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-453 were cultured in Leibovitz’s L-15 Medium. Other cell lines were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM). All normal cell lines were supplemented with 15% fetal bovine serum and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin. All cancer cell lines were supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin. For calcium-free conditions, cells were incubated in calcium-free DMEM (21068028, Invitrogen).

Reagents and antibodies
225, its structural analogs, and 225-cc were synthesized in-house. 2-Aminoethyldiphenylborinate (2-APB, HY-W009724) and BAPTA-AM (HY-100545) were purchased from MedChemExpress. Phos-tag Acrylamide AAL-107 was purchased from Fujifilm. Efsevin was purchased from A1 BioChem Labs (cas# 212070-75-2). All other chemicals and lab reagents were purchased from Millipore Sigma unless otherwise indicated. For experiments, cells were treated with 225 at the indicated concentrations for specified time periods. 225 was dissolved in DMSO (1 mM stock solution), and control experiments included an equivalent volume of DMSO (final concentration did not exceed 0.1%). Inhibitors used were added 1 h prior to treatment with 225 where indicated.

The sources of the antibodies are as follows: Anti-HA11 (ENZ-ABS120, clone 16B12, 1:500) was purchased from Enzo Lifesciences. Anti-VDAC1 (820704, clone N152B123, 1:1000) and anti-STIM1 (621702, clone W18094A, 1:1000) were obtained from Biolegend. Dislocation-induced reconstituted GFP (drGFP) assay
HeLa cells stably expressing SP-S11-NHK-HA and S1-10 (NHK-drGFP)36 were plated in 96-well plates (2×10⁴ cells/well) and cultured overnight. After replacing the medium, cells were treated with indicated concentrations of 225 and/or BTZ (2 μM). GFP fluorescence was monitored in real-time using a 20× objective on the IncuCyte S3 live-cell analysis system.

drGFP-based high-content screening
Primary screening. To identify small molecule modulators of ER dislocation, NHK-drGFP reporter-expressing HeLa cells were seeded in black low base 1536-well assay plates (EBA141000A; Aurora) at a density of ~1000 cells per well in 5 μL of Fluorobrite DMEM media (A18967-01; Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS (SH30071.03, Cytivia), 5 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin (10378-016; Gibco), 21 mM HEPES (15630-080; Gibco) and 2 mM Glutamine (25030-081; Gibco) using a Multidrop Combi reagent dispenser (5840330; Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a small tube metal tip dispensing cassette (24073295; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Plates were cultured overnight (16 h) in incubators maintained at 37°C, with 5% CO2, and 95% humidity prior to the addition of 20 nL compound (dissolved in DMSO) using a Kalypsys pintool equipped with a 1536-pin array. To monitor ER dislocation, cells were incubated for 15 minutes, then treated with 2 μL of media containing 21 μM (6 μM final) Bortezomib (S1013; SelleckChem) to promote the accumulation of NHK-drGFP following the addition of compound. Plates were then incubated for 4 h prior to GFP quantification using an Acumen EX3 Microplate Cytometer (TTPLabtech). Data was normalized to multiple replicates (n=32) of cells treated with and without bortezomib, plus an equivalent volume of DMSO. To monitor assay performance, each plate included a 16 pt titration of the p97 inhibitor, NMS-873 (HY-15713; MedChemExpress), as a reference control. Library compounds demonstrating significant reduction of GFP signal (≤60% activity relative to DMSO) were replated in 11 pt titration and re-tested, as described, to confirm inhibitory activity, generate dose-response curves and calculate AC50 values.

Secondary Assay. Compounds confirmed in dose-response follow-up testing and exhibiting select hit parameters (≤60% activity relative to DMSO controls and AC50 ≤25 μM) were then re-tested in a secondary assay employing the same stable cell line. Briefly, cells were seeded at ~1000 cells per well in ultra-low base 1536-well, 188 μM film-bottom assay plates (EBC241000A; Aurora) and treated with compound and bortezomib, as described. Following 3.75 h of incubation, each well received 1 μL of pre-warmed media containing 25 ng/mL (3.125 ng/mL final) Hoechst (H3570; Invitrogen) using a Multidrop Combi reagent dispenser (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Plates were pulse centrifuged (30 s at 1000 rpm) using a benchtop centrifuge (5804R; Eppendorf) equipped with a microplate rotor and bucket (Eppendorf; EP-2DWPAT) then incubated 15 min at room temperature prior to quantification using an InCell Analyzer 2000 Imaging Plate Reader System or Opera Phenix Plus High-Content Screening System. Acquired images were processed using a Columbus Image Data Storage and Analysis System to quantify cellular GFP based on nuclear staining and corrected for background. Data was normalized to multiple replicates (n=32) of cells treated with and without bortezomib, plus an equivalent volume of DMSO. To monitor assay performance, each plate included a 16 pt titration of the p97 inhibitor, NMS-873, as a reference control.

Establishment of gene-modified cell lines
ssRFP-GFP-KDEL stable cell line. HeLa cells were transfected with pLVX-ssRFP-GFP-KDEL plasmid using Lipofectamine 3000 (L3000015, Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s protocol. After 48 h, stable transfectants were selected with puromycin. Positive clones were maintained under puromycin selection and verified by fluorescence microscopy and Western blot analysis.

VDAC knockout cell lines. VDAC1, VDAC2, VDAC3, and VDAC2/VDAC3 knockout HeLa cell lines were generated using CRISPR-Cas9. Single-guide RNA expression plasmids (Addgene) targeting each VDAC isoform were transfected into HeLa cells cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS. Transfected cells were selected with puromycin (2 μg/mL) for 3 days. Successful knockout was confirmed by immunoblotting using isoform-specific anti-VDAC antibodies. (Primer sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 1.)

siRNA Knockdown. Negative Control siRNA was purchased from Ambion. PERK siRNA (9024S) was purchased from Cell Signaling Technology. All other siRNAs were synthesized by Millipore Sigma (Supplementary Table 2). All siRNAs were transfected with Lipofectamine® RNAiMAX transfection reagent (Invitrogen) using siRNA in Opti-MEM with no antibiotic. After 72 h of transfection, knockdown efficiency was confirmed by western blotting. Cells were then treated with 225, and downstream effects were assessed.

Cytoheximide (CHX) chase35. To measure the degradation rate and stability of NHK and CD3δ35, HeLa cells stably expressing HA-tagged NHK or CD3δ were plated and allowed to reach 70−80% confluence before initiating the chase experiment. CHX was added to the culture medium at a final concentration of 50 μg/mL to halt de novo protein synthesis. Cells were incubated with either CHX alone or along with 225 for the indicated time points. Then cells were harvested and processed for immunoblotting with anti-HA and anti-β-actin antibodies.

Immunoprecipitation (IP). Cells transfected with indicated plasmids or empty vector were treated with DMSO (control) or 225 for 3 h, then lysed in buffer (150 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris/HCl pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.2% NP-40) containing protease inhibitors. For each IP reaction, 700 μg of protein in 800 μL total volume was used. Lysates from cells expressing ectopic proteins were incubated with anti-GFP or anti-HA affinity beads for 2 h at 4°C with gentle shaking. Beads were washed three times with 700 μL lysis buffer before processing for immunoblotting (IB).

NHK ubiquitination was analyzed by re-immunoprecipitation (Re-IP)35. Briefly, HeLa cells expressing NHK-HA were treated with BTZ (2 μM) with or without 2 μM 225. Cells were then collected and lysed in (150 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris/HCl pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.2% NP-40) containing protease inhibitors, and NHK-HA was immunoprecipitated using an anti-HA affinity matrix. To eliminate non-specifically bound proteins, immunoprecipitates were denatured with 2% SDS, and beads were removed by centrifugation. The supernatants were diluted 20-fold in native lysis buffer, and NHK-HA was re-immunoprecipitated before immunoblotting for HA and ubiquitin.

Immunoblotting (IB). Total cell lysates were prepared in lysis buffer (10 mM Tris/HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.2% NP-40, 0.5% Triton X-100, pH 7.5) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking nonspecific binding sites with 5% milk for 1 h at room temperature, membranes were probed with primary antibodies, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Following TBST washes, immunoreactive bands were detected using SuperSignal West Pico PLUS or Femto Maximum Sensitivity chemiluminescent substrates.

Caspase-3/7 activity assay. Apoptosis was assessed using the IncuCyte® Caspase-3/7 Green Apoptosis Assay. HeLa cells were treated with 225 at the indicated concentrations in the presence of the caspase-3/7 reagent (1:2000 dilution). Fluorescence intensity, reflecting caspase-3/7 activity, was measured in real-time using the IncuCyte® S3 system.

Target identification using photoaffinity and clickable 225 and Mass Spectrometry (MS). Cells were cultured to ~80% confluence and incubated with 5 μM of 225-cc in the presence or absence of 80 μM 225 for 30 min at 37°C to allow compound binding to target proteins. After incubation, cells were rinsed with PBS and irradiated with UV light (355 nm) for 20 minutes on ice to covalently crosslink probe 225-cc to its interacting proteins. Following crosslinking, cells were washed with cold PBS and lysed in 1% NP40 buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 10% Glycerol, 1% NP40) containing EDTA free protease inhibitor cocktail. The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C, and protein concentration was determined. Urea was then added to cleared lysate (~680 mg urea to 1 mL lysate) to achieve a final urea concentration of approximately 8 M.

For pull-down assay, 1.3 mL of the urea-denatured lysate (~1.5 mg proteins) was mixed with the following reagents: 30 μL of 1 mM Dde-TAMRA-Biotin-Azide (Click Chemistry Tools, 1367-1), 70 μL of 100 mM THPTA, 14 μL of 100 mM CuSO4 and 70 μL of 300 mM sodium ascorbate. The click reaction mixture was incubated for 30 min at room temperature in the dark on a rotator. Following incubation, proteins were precipitated by cold methanol and chloroform. Precipitated proteins were resuspended in 1% SDS, 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), and 150 mM NaCl, followed by sonication. Each sample was incubated with 50 μL Pierce™ Streptavidin Magnetic Beads (Thermo Fisher, 88816) for 1.5 h at room temperature. Beads were washed three times with the same resuspension buffer. After washing, beads were boiled in SDS loading buffer containing 5 mM biotin and proceeded to SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting if applicable. For mass spectrometry analysis, fluorescent bands at ~35 kDa (both 225-cc and with competition control by adding free 225) and ~18 kDa (only 225-cc) were excised (3 gel pieces in total, N=1 for each condition) and cut into 1 mm pieces. Gel pieces were washed twice with 50% methanol for 10 minutes each, then the gel pieces were stored at −20°C prior to LC-MS/MS analysis. The click reaction can be scale down to 50 μL total volume with 50 μg proteins when the sample is only used for fluorescent visualization of the probe-labeled proteins in the SDS-PAGE gel.

For gel band excision, clean and sterile razors were used to cut the desired band/slice in a process-protection hood. The slice was further cut into 1×1 mm pieces prior to de-staining, reduction and alkylation, tryptic digestion and peptide extraction81. In brief, 1×1 mm gel pieces were transferred into pre-rinsed 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes and re-swelled in 50 µL of 20 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC), followed by dehydration with 50 µL of acetonitrile. After discarding the solvent, the gel pieces were re-swelled in 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) and incubated for 1 h at 56°C for reduction, followed by alkylation with 55 mM iodoacetamide (IAA) for 45 min at room temperature in the dark. The solution was discarded, and the gel pieces were washed with 50 mM ABC and dehydrated again with acetonitrile. After the final dehydration step, the gels were dried completely using a SpeedVac. The dried gel pieces were then re-swelled on ice for 45–60 min in 25 µL of 10 ng/µL trypsin prepared in 20 mM ABC. Excess trypsin solution was removed, and the gel pieces were covered with 25 µL of 20 mM ABC and incubated overnight at 37°C for digestion. Peptides were extracted once with 25 µL of 20 mM ABC and three times with 50 µL of 50% acetonitrile containing 5% formic acid. All supernatants were combined and lyophilized by speed-vac and resuspended in 2% acetonitrile, 97.9% water, and 0.1% formic acid buffer for liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis. The LC-MS/MS analysis of in-gel digested product was performed using an UltiMate 3000-nano LC system coupled to the Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer equipped with the Nanospray Flex ion source (Thermo Fisher). Peptides were loaded onto the trap column (Acclaim PepMap 100 C18, 75 μm × 2 cm, particle size: 3 μm, 100 Å; Thermo Fisher) by autosampler using loading solvent (2% acetonitrile in MS-grade water, 0.1% FA) at a flow rate of 4 μL/min. Elution of peptides from the analytical column (with spray tip, 75 μm × 20 cm, 1.7 μm, 100 Å; CoAnn Technologies) was performed using a 60 min method (~45 min gradient) starting at 98% solution A (0.1% formic acid in MS-grade water) at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. The mobile phase was maintained at 2% solution B (80% acetonitrile, 19.9% water, 0.1% formic acid) for 5 min, 2–9% B for 2 min, 9–38% B for 33 min, 38–50% B for 2 min, 50–90% B for 3 min, and maintained at 90% B for 6 min, followed by re-equilibration of the column with 2% B for 7 min. Column oven temperature was set as 40°C. The mass spectrometer was operated in positive-ionization mode with spray voltage set at 1800 V, and ion transfer tube temperature set at 250°C. The MS scan was operated at data-dependent acquisition mode, with full MS scans over a mass range of m/z 375–1800 with detection in the Orbitrap (120K resolution) and with auto gain control (AGC) set to 1.0×106. The fragment ion spectra were acquired in Orbitrap (15K resolution) with a normalized collision energy of 28% at HCD activation mode. In each cycle of data-dependent acquisition analysis, the most intense ions were selected for the MS/MS analysis, and the cycle time for MS and MS/MS analysis was set as 2 s. The AGC for MS/MS was set as 5.0×104 and the maximum injection time was 22 ms. Precursor ions with charges of +2 to +7 were isolated for MS/MS sequencing. The MS/MS isolation window was 1.2 Da, and the dynamic exclusion time was set at 60 s with a mass tolerance of ±10 ppm.

Proteome Discoverer software suite (version 3.0, Thermo Fisher) with Sequest algorithm was used for peptide identification. The MS raw data were searched against a Swiss-Prot human database (version November 2022, reviewed database) consisting of 20,328 entries using the following parameters: precursor ion mass tolerance of 10 ppm and a fragment ion mass tolerance of 0.02 Da. Peptides were searched using fully tryptic cleavage constraints and up to two internal cleavage sites were allowed for tryptic digestion. Fixed modifications consisted of carbamidomethylation of cysteine. Variable modifications considered were oxidation of methionine residues. Peptide identification false discovery rates (FDR) were limited to a maximum of 0.01 using identifications from a concatenated database from the non-decoy and the decoy databases. Minimum number of peptide for protein identification was set as 1 and protein was ranked by number of PSMs.

Differential expression and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)82. Differential expression analysis between 225-treated and untreated samples (three biological replicates per group) was first performed using the DESeq2 R package (v1.14.1), which models digital gene expression data with a negative binomial distribution. Genes with a p value < 0.05 were designated as differentially expressed and were subsequently ranked based on their expression changes to serve as input for gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). GSEA was then performed using the GSEA software (v4.4.0, available at http://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp) with default parameters to identify biological pathways and transcriptional programs regulated by compound 225. Pre-defined gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB), including the Hallmark and KEGG collections, were evaluated, and pathways with a false discovery rate (FDR)–adjusted p-value < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched. The normalized enrichment score (NES) was used to quantify the degree of enrichment for each gene set82.

Microscale thermophoresis (MST). Recombinant human VDAC1 bearing an N-terminal His-tag (Proteogenix, Cat#: ARO-P13933) was equilibrated on ice for 1 h in PBS (pH 7.4) supplemented with 0.05% n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM). His-tag–directed fluorescent labeling was performed using the RED-tris-NTA 2nd Generation dye (NanoTemper, Cat#: MO-L018) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The high-affinity interaction between His-tags and tris-NTA (~1–10 nM) ensured selective labeling without additional purification. To determine the binding affinity of compound 225 for VDAC1, a two-fold serial dilution of 225 was prepared in PBS containing 0.05% DDM, starting at 100 µM to generate a twelve-point titration series. Fluorescently labeled protein (10 µL, final concentration 50 nM) was mixed with 10 µL of each 225 concentration, resulting in a maximal compound concentration of 50 µM. Samples were incubated for 30 min at room temperature and loaded into Monolith Premium Capillaries (NanoTemper, Cat#: MO-K025). Two independent replicate measurements were collected for each concentration.

MST measurements were acquired using a Monolith X instrument (NanoTemper Technologies GmbH) with high IR-laser power and automatic excitation settings. MST response values were automatically converted to “fraction bound” in MO. Control software (v2.7.1). Duplicate measurements at each concentration were averaged, and the averaged values were used to generate the binding curve. The dissociation constant (Kd) was determined by nonlinear regression using the MO. Control software.

Cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA)55,56. CETSA was employed to evaluate compound–protein engagement in cells55,56. HeLa cells were seeded and allowed to adhere, then treated with 2 μM compound 225 or an equivalent volume of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) at 37°C for 1 h. After treatment, cells were harvested by scraping and lysed in buffer (150 mM NaCl, 10 mM Tris/HCl pH 7.4, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 0.4% NP-40) supplemented with protease inhibitors. The lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 14,000 × g for 10 min, and protein concentrations of the resulting supernatants were determined and normalized across samples. Normalized aliquots of the lysates were heated at the indicated temperatures for 3 min, followed by cooling to room temperature (25°C) for 3 min. The samples were then centrifuged at 20,000 × g for 20 min to separate soluble proteins from precipitated aggregates. Soluble fractions were mixed with 4× SDS sample buffer and subjected to immunoblotting.

VDAC1 gating. Planar lipid bilayers were made by the apposition of two monolayers comprised of the 1:1 (w:w) mixture of 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC) and 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (DOPE) lipids (Avanti Polar Lipids, Alabaster, AL) dissolved in pentane. These monolayers were formed across a ∼125 μm (in multichannel experiments) and 75 μm (in single channel experiments) diameter aperture within a 15-μm-thick Teflon film separating two ∼1.5-mL compartments filled with 1 M KCl solution buffered by 5 mM HEPES at pH 7.4, as previously described64. The recombinant human VDAC1 was a generous gift of Tsyr-Yan Dharma Yu (Institute of Atomic and Molecular Sciences, Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan). VDAC1 channel insertion was obtained after addition of 0.2–0.5 μl of VDAC1 diluted in 100 mM Tris, 50 mM KCl, 1 mM EDTA, 15% (v/v) DMSO, 2.5% (v/v) Triton X-100, pH 7.35 to the cis compartment of the experimental chamber while stirring. The procedure of VDAC reconstitution into lipid bilayers was described previously64,83. Potential is defined as positive when it is greater on the cis side, the side of compound 225 and VDAC1 addition.

Ion current recordings were acquired using an Axopatch 200B amplifier (Axon Instruments) in voltage clamp mode, following previously reported protocols83. Current signals were filtered at 10 kHz with a low-pass Bessel filter, digitized at a sampling frequency of 50 kHz, and analyzed using pClamp 10.7 software (Axon Instruments). For single-channel analyses in Clampfit 10.7, recordings were further digitally filtered with a 5 kHz 8-pole Bessel low-pass filter.

Voltage-dependence of VDAC gating was analyzed using a previously described protocol63,64 under the application of a slow, symmetric triangular voltage wave (±60 mV, 5 mHz) generated by an Arbitrary Waveform Generator 33220A (Agilent Technologies). Data were sampled at 2 Hz frequency and analyzed as detailed earlier63 using a custom in-house algorithm and pClamp 10.7 software. In each experiment, current records were collected from membranes containing 10-50 channels in response to 5–10 periods of voltage waves to ensure data collection from more than 50 channels per experiment. Only the part of the wave, during which the channels were reopening, was used for the subsequent analysis for the reasons described elsewhere63.

Xenograft. The A375 human melanoma cell line was maintained in high-glucose DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. Compound 225 was formulated in a vehicle consisting of N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, polyethyleneglycol 300, propylene glycol, and 20% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin. Male BALB/c-nu mice (7 weeks old) were housed in a specific pathogen-free facility under standard conditions. We fully acknowledge the journal’s policy on sex inclusion and recognize the importance of sex as a biological variable. In our initial in vivo proof-of-principle study, only male BALB/c-nu mice were used to minimize biological variability and obtain clear efficacy data. This design avoided estrous cycle–related hormonal fluctuations that can influence tumor growth and pharmacokinetics, following standard early-stage oncology practice to isolate treatment effects. Our approach aligns with the NIH Sex as a Biological Variable policy (NOT-OD-15-102), which permits single-sex studies when scientifically justified, and with the FDA Modernization Act 2.0 and FDA 2025 Roadmap for Reducing Animal Testing, which emphasize refinement and reduction of animal use when feasible. Future studies will include both sexes and incorporate non-animal models, consistent with evolving NIH and FDA guidance promoting rigor, reproducibility, and responsible animal research. Log-phase A375 cells (2×10⁶) were suspended in a 1:1 mixture with Matrigel and injected subcutaneously into the right flank (n=8 per group). After 7 days, mice received daily intraperitoneal injections of 225 (20 mg/kg) or vehicle. Tumor size was measured every two days using calipers, and tumor volume was calculated as (a×b²)/2, where a and b represent the longest and shortest perpendicular diameters, respectively. On day 21, mice were euthanized, and tumors and major organs were collected for histological analysis. All animal procedures were performed in accordance with institutional guidelines and approved by the Experimental Animal Ethics Committee of the Institute of Clinical Pharmacology, Anhui Medical University (Approval No. PZ-2021-016).

Statistical analysis. All quantitative data presented are representative of at least three independent experiments. Data are shown as means ± SD. Differences between two groups were analyzed by unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test using GraphPad Prism 7.0. For all analyses, the p-value was considered significant as follows: **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001. Data visualization was performed using GraphPad Prism and the ggplot2 package (version 3.5.1) in R (version 4.4.3).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

General Assessment:
Yan et al. describe the identification of NCATS-SM0225 as an ERAD inhibitor via a GFP-based HTS and elucidate its
mechanism involving VDAC binding, dysregulation of calcium homeostasis, and selective cancer cell cytotoxicity. While the
study identifies a novel compound with an intriguing mechanism and therapeutic potential, several critical conclusions lack
sufficient experimental validation. The mechanistic claims require substantial reinforcement to meet the journal's standards.
Major revisions addressing the following points are essential prior to reconsideration.
Major Concerns:
1. HTS Compound Prioritization Rationale: The manuscript states that 6 compounds were prioritized from 62 initial hits for
further study. The specific criteria (e.g., potency, chemical tractability, structural diversity, lack of known liabilities) guiding
this selection must be explicitly defined. Without this justification, the rationale for focusing on SM0225 remains unclear and
potentially arbitrary.
2. Mechanism of STIM1-PERK Affinity Enhancement (Fig 8e): The observation that SM0225 enhances endogenous STIM1-
PERK affinity is significant. However, as SM0225 is not proposed to directly bind either protein, the underlying mechanism
for this effect remains entirely speculative. The authors must propose and experimentally test a plausible mechanism (e.g.,
involving Ca²⁺ flux, ER stress sensor activation, or intermediary adaptors) or significantly temper their interpretation of this
result.
3. Clarity on ERAD Reporter Substrate (Fig 1e): The misfolded CD3δ-based drGFP reporter used for secondary HTS
validation must be clearly defined upon its first mention in the main text (HTS section). Ensure consistent nomenclature
between text and Fig 1e.
4. Validation of VDAC1-3 Binding: The identification of VDAC1-3 as targets via photoaffinity labeling (PAL) and SDS-
PAGE/MS is a key finding. However, confirmation using orthogonal, quantitative biophysical methods is crucial to establish
binding affinity, specificity, and stoichiometry. Strongly recommend performing Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA)
combined with either Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) or Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) to validate and quantify
the direct interaction between SM0225 and VDAC isoforms 1-3. Relying solely on PAL (inherently detecting covalent
interactions) is insufficient proof of the physiological, non-covalent binding implied in the proposed mechanism.
5. Incomplete Exploration of Differential Cell Sensitivity: The differential sensitivity of cancer cell lines to SM0225 is a
compelling observation with translational relevance. However, the exploration of the proposed mechanism (involving
ERAD/ER-phagy crosstalk) is superficial. To validate the hypothesis that ER-phagy capacity dictates sensitivity, the authors
should inhibit ER-phagy (e.g., via genetic knockdown of key regulators like FAM134B, SEC62, or CCPG1, or using
pharmacological inhibitors like CQ/HCQ where appropriate) in resistant/low-sensitivity cell lines and assess whether this
sensitizes them to SM0225-induced cytotoxicity. Demonstrating this functional link is essential to support the model in
Figure 9.
6. Lack of In Vivo Efficacy and Safety Data: Demonstrating potent and selective cancer cell killing in vitro is promising, but in
vivo validation is a fundamental requirement for a mechanistic/therapeutic study of this nature in Nature Communications.
The authors should provide evidence of SM0225's efficacy in relevant tumor xenograft or syngeneic models, alongside
assessment of toxicity in normal tissues. This is critical for establishing the compound's therapeutic window and translational
potential.

### Reviewer 2

In this study by Yan et al., the authors developed a chemical screening platform based on an ERAD dislocation reporter. The
screen identified compound 225 as a small-molecule ERAD inhibitor. They further dissected the mechanism of action of 225
by identifying the VDACs as the drug targets, demonstrating disruption of calcium homeostasis, and linking the
PERK/STIM1 axis to degradation of ERAD complex proteins and cell death. Overall, this is an interesting study that provides
novel insights into the regulation of UPR, calcium homeostasis, ERAD, and ER-phagy.
Several minor comments are listed below:
1. Figure 3a: The authors mentioned the degradation of OS9, HERP1, and FAM8A1. However, the data also show a
reduction in SEL1L at 24 hours post-treatment. This should also be noted in the text.
2. Figure 3: The authors should examine transcriptomic changes in the RNA-seq data for OS9, HERP1, FAM8A1, and
SEL1L mRNA levels to rule out mRNA downregulation as the cause of decreased protein levels.
3. Figures 2d–g and 4i: Treatment with 225 significantly inhibited the degradation of both NHK and CD3, resulting in
increased protein levels. However, in Figure 4i, siVDAC1 treatment reduced CD3-mCherry levels. These findings seem
inconsistent and should be clarified.
4. The term “dislocation” should be defined earlier in the manuscript for clarity.

### Reviewer 3

Yan and colleagues present compelling evidence that stress-induced apoptosis in cancer cells can be increased by
suppressing the Endoplasmic Reticulum-Associated Degradation (ERAD) pathway using small molecules. Through an
extensive drug screening campaign employing a clever designed readout, they identified novel ERAD inhibitors. One of the
most potent molecules identified, compound 225, not only inhibits ERAD but also binds the mitochondrial porin VDAC1.
While a direct link between VDAC1 and the ERAD pathway has not been conclusively established before, the authors
provide strong evidence supporting VDAC1 involvement in ERAD regulation.
The manuscript is data-rich and covers several key aspects, including the drug screening process, interaction studies (IP
experiments), and mechanistic insights that collectively support the proposed conclusions. However, I have several
important questions and concerns that should be addressed prior to publication:
Major Points:
1. The authors demonstrate that compound 225 stabilizes the interaction between VDAC1 and the IP3 receptor. Do the
authors have mechanistic insights or supporting data explaining why this interaction is enhanced in the presence of
molecule 225? Is this effect direct, or could it result from broader changes in organelle physiology?
2. Compound 225 appears to have dual effects: it activates PERK, resulting in STIM1 phosphorylation, HERP1 degradation,
and ERAD inhibition; while also binding to VDAC1. However, UV-crosslinking identified VDACs as the only direct targets.
How do the authors reconcile this dual activity? Is there evidence that the STIM1–PERK interaction is influenced by the
VDAC–IP3R complex? Could the authors attempt IP experiments to pull down VDAC using STIM1 or PERK in the presence
of 225 to test for complex formation?
3. The manuscript claims that molecule 225 selectively targets cancer cells without affecting healthy cells. Given that
VDAC1 is overexpressed in many solid tumors, did the authors assess VDAC1 expression levels in 225-sensitive versus -
insensitive cell lines? Quantifying VDAC1 levels by RNA-seq and Western blot would help clarify whether sensitivity to 225
correlates with VDAC1 expression and might explain the lack of toxicity in healthy cells.
4. The authors propose that molecule 225 enhances VDAC1–IP3R interaction, promoting calcium transfer between the ER
and mitochondria, which subsequently activates PERK and drives ERAD inhibition. However, this does not fully explain the
observed increase in cytosolic calcium (Fig. 7c). Could the authors comment on the source of the cytosolic calcium and
clarify whether this increase is a direct or indirect consequence of 225 treatment?
5. The small molecule efsevin has been shown to stabilize the calcium-conductive form of VDAC1 (PMID: 32059260). It
would be informative to compare the effects of efsevin and compound 225 on ERAD inhibition. Do both compounds share a
similar mechanism of action? Such a comparison might strengthen the proposed model.
Minor Points:
Scheme on Figure 8j should be revised to clearly depict relevant subcellular compartments, improve image quality, and
remove the pink background. Additionally, the graph located at the bottom left appears to be an error and should be
removed.

### Reviewer 4

Key Results
This manuscript identifies a novel small molecule, NCATS-SM0225 (“225”), as a selective ERAD inhibitor that binds to
voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs). Through a combination of high-content screening, biochemical validation, and
mechanistic dissection, the authors suggest that 225 triggers an intracellular calcium imbalance via a VDAC-IP3R-PERK-
STIM1 signaling axis. This leads to the degradation of ERAD complex components (HERP1, OS9, FAM8A1) and induces
cell death selectively in cancer cells while sparing normal cells. The work uncovers a previously unrecognized role for
VDACs in ERAD regulation and presents a compelling chemical probe for further study of ER proteostasis and cancer-
selective cytotoxicity.
Validity
The data are of high quality, robust, and generally well-controlled. The experimental workflow is thorough, including
orthogonal validation of dislocation inhibition (GFP reporters, CHX chase, ubiquitination assays), target identification
(photoaffinity labeling and MS), and functional studies using gene knockouts and chemical inhibitors. However, the precise
mechanism of 225 binding to VDACs and how this affects VDAC function at a structural level remains speculative. The
authors acknowledge this and propose it as future work.
Significance
The identification of a VDAC-targeting small molecule that selectively disrupts ERAD and kills cancer cells is novel and
potentially impactful. This work opens new avenues in cancer biology, proteostasis, and chemical biology. It also proposes
an alternative strategy to targeting UPR sensors directly — by modulating ERAD upstream. The selective toxicity of 225 to
certain cancer cell lines suggests translational relevance. While the mechanistic basis of this selectivity is not fully resolved,
the dataset lays a solid foundation for follow-up studies.
Data and Methodology
The methodology is state-of-the-art and spans a wide range of experimental techniques, including high-content screening,
SAR chemistry, CRISPR knockouts, calcium imaging, and GSEA transcriptomic profiling. The description of materials and
methods is detailed and transparent. Use of the drGFP reporter for dislocation, combined with dose-responses, time
courses, and structure–activity relationships, makes the data solid. Photoaffinity labeling with mass spectrometry is well
executed, and VDAC target identification is convincing. If available, raw calcium traces or proteomics data could be made
public in supplementary datasets.
Analytical Approach
Quantitative results are consistently supported by replicates, appropriate statistical tests, and careful normalization. The use
of dose-response curves, IC50 values, and multiple replicates is appropriate. GSEA is correctly applied and complements
the mechanistic data. The authors have been transparent about sample sizes and statistical significance thresholds.
Suggested Improvements
The authors present a compelling study identifying VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as direct binding partners of compound
225. They propose that 225 perturbs calcium homeostasis at the ER-mitochondria interface via these outer mitochondrial
membrane proteins, thereby inhibiting ER-associated degradation (ERAD), activating the unfolded protein response (UPR),
and triggering apoptosis. While the data are generally sound and well-presented, I believe an alternative, structurally
grounded interpretation offers a more parsimonious explanation of the experimental findings.
Recent structural studies (Li et al., Aging 2023, DOI:10.18632/aging.205660) demonstrate that VDAC1 directly binds the ER
membrane protein complex (EMC) at ER-mitochondria contact sites (MAMs), locking the EMC in a non-insertase
conformation.
Earlier proteomic mapping
(Christianson, J., Olzmann, J., Shaler, T. et al. Defining human ERAD networks through an integrative mapping strategy. Nat
Cell Biol 14, 93–105 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1038/ncb2383)
showed that multiple EMC subunits interact with Derlin-1 and Derlin-2, core components of the ERAD dislocation
machinery. This raises the possibility that compound 225 inhibits ERAD not by modulating VDAC channel activity directly,
but by stabilizing a non-functional EMC–VDAC complex that disrupts EMC-dependent membrane insertion of ERAD
components such as Derlin-1.
Below, I analyze the major data types presented by the authors in support of their model and offer the alternative EMC-
mediated interpretation.
1. Identification of VDAC1/2/3 as targets of 225:
The authors used a clickable photoaffinity analog of 225 to identify VDAC1, VDAC2, and VDAC3 as binding targets.
This result is compatible with both their interpretation (VDAC as a functional target for calcium flux regulation) and my alternative
model (VDACs as structural partners of EMC, mediating 225 activity via this complex).
2. Inhibition of ERAD and activation of UPR by 225:
225 blocks degradation of NHK and HA-DeltaF508CFTR, canonical ERAD substrates. It also induces expression of BiP,
CHOP, and ATF4. The authors ascribe this to ER calcium dysregulation. However, a simpler model is that 225-bound
VDAC stabilizes EMC in a non-insertase state, blocking the membrane integration of Derlin-1 and other EMC-dependent
ERAD components, thereby directly impairing ERAD and triggering proteostatic stress. This hypothesis explains all
observed consequences (ERAD block, UPR, cell death) without invoking a poorly defined Ca2+ channeling role for VDACs.
3. Triple VDAC1 KD / VDAC2⁻/⁻ / VDAC3⁻/⁻ cells resist 225 phenotypes:
The authors interpret this as evidence that VDACs are the functional conduits for calcium flux perturbed by 225.
However, in the alternative model, the absence of VDACs prevents 225 from stabilizing the EMC–VDAC complex. This
restores EMC function and Derlin-1 insertion, preserving ERAD and preventing downstream UPR and Ca2+
dysregulation. Thus, the triple KO phenotype is compatible with both models.
4. ER calcium flux and 225-induced cell death:
Calcium flux is clearly altered by 225, but the authors do not provide direct electrophysiological or structural evidence that
225 opens or blocks VDAC pores. Given that VDAC is primarily known as a metabolite channel in the outer mitochondrial
membrane, and that Ca2+ flow between ER and mitochondria typically involves IP3R-GRP75-VDAC tethers, it remains
uncertain whether VDAC alone mediates Ca2+ leak. In contrast, the EMC-centered model predicts that ER stress and UPR
activation are primary, and that calcium dysregulation is a downstream effect of ER proteostasis failure.
Conclusion:
In light of published structural and proteomic data, the model in which compound 225 exerts its effects by stabilizing a non-
insertase EMC–VDAC complex provides a mechanistically unified explanation of all observed phenotypes: ERAD
inhibition, UPR activation, and calcium flux. It avoids invoking a direct gating effect of 225 on VDACs, for which no structural
or biophysical support is currently provided. I suggest the authors consider this alternative mechanism in the discussion and
test whether EMC activity or Derlin-1 insertion is altered upon 225 treatment.
This model is not incompatible with the authors' data, but may better contextualize the role of VDACs as structural, rather
than purely channel, components at MAMs. It also makes distinct predictions about EMC dependency that could be
experimentally tested.
Suggested experiments:
Assess Derlin-1 levels and membrane insertion after 225 treatment
Test EMC–VDAC complex stability or conformation changes in the presence of 225
Compare 225 sensitivity in cells with EMC subunit knockdown or mutation
Clarity and Context
The manuscript is clearly written and accessible. Figures are well designed and support the main conclusions. The
discussion appropriately contextualizes the findings within existing literature and discusses limitations transparently. The
novelty of VDACs in ERAD is well supported.
References
The referencing is thorough and appropriate. Key prior work on ERAD, UPR, VDAC function, and chemical screening is
cited. I did not note any major omissions.
Your Expertise
My expertise includes ER proteostasis and chemical biology. I am confident in assessing the main findings and mechanistic
claims. I did not independently evaluate the full MS data or chemical synthesis protocols but found the presented validation
to be sufficient.
